articles.title: Carney says US trying to break Canada amid vote for Alberta independence referendum
articles.summary: The oil-rich province of Alberta will vote to decide if it wants to remain a Canadian province or start the legal process toward separation. Carney warned that the US was trying the divide-and-rule…

image.caption: Mark Carney was campaigning at a pro-Canada rally in Alberta ahead of next week's voteImage: Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned the people of oil-rich Alberta that the United States was trying to break Canada so it could "own us."
Carney was speaking at a pro-Canada rally in Calgary, ahead of a vote which will decide if the disgruntled western province will begin a legal process towards separation from Canada.
"The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us," he said, without naming the US or its president, Donald Trump.
This is not the first time Carney has made such a claim. His warning comes as Washington and Ottawa are in the middle of a trade war and Trump has threatened to make Canada the 51st US state.
Meanwhile, Carney's push towards making Canada less dependent on the US has irked Trump.
How could Trump react to Canada-EU association plan?
What is is Alberta voting for?

Monday's vote in Alberta is not a direct referendum on independence. Rather, the province, which has the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will vote to decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process towards a referendum on separation.

Albertans have long held grievances with liberal governments in Ottawa, from concerns about immigration and federal power to oil industry management. While Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has attempted to address frustrations, a lot stands to be resolved.

blocks.caption: Mark Carney grew up in AlbertaImage: Mike Sturk/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real," Carney said, adding that Ottawa had made Albertans feel "like our resources weren't our own."
However, he urged the public there to not use the vote as a "message" to the federal government.

"Don't be fooled by the idea you can 'send a message' with your vote," Carney said. "This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty."

Mitch Sylvestre, who heads the Alberta Prosperity Project, a prominent separatist organization, told AFP that US interests "don't play a role" in Alberta "until we win and become a government." At that point, he would ensure free-flowing trade.
"There is no animosity towards America here," he said, adding that he didn't see a reason to stop trading with the world's largest economy.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta a "natural partner" for the United States, and Alberta Prosperity Project leaders have held several meetings at the State Department.

articles.title: College football player Tyler Ulrich dies five days after ‘traumatic injury’ during game
articles.summary:
• 21-year-old was treated on field after injury during game

  • Coach pays tribute to player’s ‘quiet strength’

Southern Nazarene University in Oklahoma announced…

blocks.text: Southern Nazarene University in Oklahoma announced on Thursday that sophomore safety Tyler Ulrich has died five days after sustaining what the school called a “traumatic injury” during a game against Ouachita Baptist. Ulrich was 21.

The Division II school based in Bethany, Oklahoma, did not reveal the cause of death or the nature of Ulrich’s injury. Ulrich was hurt during a 49-14 loss on Saturday, with the game delayed for nearly an hour while he received medical attention before being transported to a hospital.

“It is with heavy hearts that we share the loss of our SNU football player, Tyler Ulrich,” the SNU Athletics said in a post on its X account. “This loss is deeply felt across our campus. Our hearts are with his family, friends, teammates, and everyone who knew him. We ask that you join us in lifting them up in prayer.”
SNU coach Dustin Hada also posted a tribute on X: “Man of God, ultimate example of quiet strength, loyal, worker, joyous. That’s who Tyler was!!”
The school’s president, Keith Newman, said Ulrich died in the hospital “surrounded by the love, prayers, and presence of his family, teammates and dear friends.”
On Tuesday, SNU held a campuswide prayer chapel in honor of Ulrich.
Ulrich, who was from Azle, Texas, was in his third season at SNU and had 16 starts in 20 games, including six starts this year. He ranked third on the team with 36 tackles.
Southern Nazarene have canceled their game at Southwestern Oklahoma State on Saturday.

Its services gave Israel’s Candiru — a spyware company blacklisted by the US government — as well as other Israeli surveillance firms access to advertising platforms run by Google, Comcast, Russia’s Yandex and others, according to separate reports from Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab and New York advertising security firm Confiant.

“The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat,” Wolfie Christl, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab, told Reuters. “For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike.”
Discover-Tech’s online ads — often for ordinary products such as phones or earbuds — reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said.

Users who visited sites or used apps with the malicious ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes also try to extract phone numbers from some smartphone users, the researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur.

Some ads would be used to help plant spyware from Candiru on users’ devices, both research groups said, though Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech’s overall volume.

Confiant cofounder Jerome Dangu said Discover-Tech was pumping out at least 10 million ads per day all around the world and that data-sharing arrangements — called cookie matching — allowed it to track people even beyond the reach of its advertisements.
“Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech,” Dangu said.
Discover-Tech, which was founded in 2020, did not return messages left via its contact form. A LinkedIn message and emails sent to its chief executive, Dekel Boni, were not returned.

Reuters’ attempts to reach Candiru’s owners were similarly unsuccessful. The US Commerce Department blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for allegedly supplying spyware that was used to maliciously target government officials, journalists, activists and academics.

Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech’s ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025, something it said it was able to confirm because the media group had shared its network logs with the group.

In a statement, Al Jazeera said it “condemns the spyware attacks targeting a number of its staff” and that it was taking steps to protect its employees and its systems. “Those responsible must be held accountable,” it said.

Dangu of Confiant said that the malicious ads had been shown to users in “hundreds of networks in sensitive categories,” including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, like the Palestinian territories, were particularly saturated by the Israeli firm’s ads.
“You go to almost any site in Palestine — any site — you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country,” he said.

Citizen Lab also said it had similar evidence showing the malicious ads were shown to people in the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission, and more than a dozen national governments. Other networks the ads appeared in included chip-related firms such as Nvidia, Sandisk, Broadcom, and Micron, as well as several media organizations in Mexico, Israel, and Europe that were not identified.

In addition to identifying Candiru and a couple of other surveillance vendors, Citizen Lab said it was able to glean some details about where Discover-Tech’s users might be based because the firm inadvertently exposed its authentication logs to the internet, showing people logging in from internet protocol addresses in Israel, Europe, and the Gulf.
Discover-Tech is now being frozen out of parts of the online ad market.
Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant’s investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms “for systematically violating our policies.”

IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved vendors last week after an audit identified policy violations.
Comcast ad tech subsidiary Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its platform “following recent activity,” Comcast said in a statement. Yandex did not return Reuters messages seeking comment.

Advertising-driven surveillance is increasingly being seen as a national security threat. Earlier this year, the Pentagon said it had received reports that US forces deployed to ​war zones had been targeted using location data harvested by ad tech firms and data brokers. Branches of the military have since disabled ad tracking on some devices. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Number of cloned number plates on UK roads at record high, data shows
articles.summary:
More than 11,400 drivers last year were fined for offences they did not recognise as RAC says system needs reform

The number of reported “cloned” vehicles involved in offences on UK roads…

blocks.text: The number of reported “cloned” vehicles involved in offences on UK roads has reached a record high, official data shows.

More than 11,400 drivers contacted the DVLA last year after being issued with fines for offences they said they did not recognise or accept responsibility for – most of which are believed to be down to cloning, where a number plate is copied fraudulently on similar vehicles to avoid enforcement cameras.

The number of complaints about misattribution was 9% higher than in 2024 and almost double the figure recorded in 2018, according to the RAC motoring organisation, which analysed data obtained under freedom of information requests.
The rising figures underscore concerns about the number of illegal number plates in use, allowing criminals to evade detection and dangerous drivers to avoid being caught.

Although drivers should provide number plate suppliers with the V5C vehicle logbook and proof of identity, an investigation last year uncovered more than 130 official suppliers in the UK willing to sell cloned versions, which allow drivers to dodge police and congestion charges.
Cloning vehicles has left many innocent car owners having to struggle to prove they were not responsible when enforcement camera images apparently caught their vehicle committing offences.

A parallel concern is the use of “ghost” plates which are designed to be unreadable by the UK’s 18,000 automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) cameras, which enforce safety measures such as speed limits or lane closures on smart motorways.

The RAC said the UK needed to overhaul an outdated and poorly regulated number plate system. Its head of policy, Simon Williams, said: “If number plate suppliers were carrying out all the checks they’re supposed to, it would be much harder for dodgy drivers to buy cloned plates in the first place. It’s only when a fine arrives at a vehicle keeper’s home address that they realise someone else is driving around using their vehicle’s number plate illegally.”

He said that more also needed to be done to catch drivers with ghost plates, “whether that’s more police officers being equipped with handheld devices that can detect if plates are unreadable, updating ANPR cameras and introducing higher security standards for number plates and for those who produce them”.

The government last month said there would be a new nationwide crackdown on illegal number plates, with funding from the Department for Transport for a new roads policing team. A new National Roads Policing Coordination Centre would share intelligence as well as trialling new technology such as specialised goggles to detect number plates that have been designed to be unreadable by cameras.
after newsletter promotion
Drivers using an incorrectly displayed number plate can be fined up to £1,000.

A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “We’re cracking down on illegal number plates with significant investment in a new roads policing team and innovative tech to stamp out the scourge of cloned numberplates.
“Illegal number plates help facilitate crime, and we are supporting the police to work with the DVLA to make it easier to report these crimes and support victims through a new digital tool.”

articles.title: Future of western security is at stake in Yemen civil war, says country’s former PM
articles.summary:
Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed says Iran-backed militia’s use of drones represents ‘new era of radical terrorism’

The future of western security is being fought out in the mountains and hills…

blocks.text: The future of western security is being fought out in the mountains and hills surrounding the south-western Yemeni city of Taiz, the country’s former prime minster has said.

Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed, now an adviser to Yemen’s president, said it would be catastrophic if the city fell to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, since control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait in the Red Sea and the road to Aden – the site of the UN-recognised government – would be lost.
Appealing for more western help, Saeed said he had no doubt that the Houthis intended to seize control of all of Yemen, and claimed their goal was “to help Iran to expand the chaos”.

blocks.caption: Houthis ride in a funeral procession for their fellow fighters in Sana’a, Yemen, in September. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA

blocks.text: Saeed admitted the lack of coordination among government-backed troops, competition between Gulf states and a slowness to appreciate the implications of Yemen acquiring long-range drone technology had contributed to the pressure facing his government, and its chief backer Saudi Arabia.
“We only have light weapons and Saudi Arabia did not plan at an early stage for this escalation, but it is never too late to regain our position,” he said.
Saeed called on the west to think through the implications of allowing the Houthis to take control of Yemen, arguing the country would never be secure with Houthis on the land.
Saeed is not only an adviser to the Yemeni president, Rashad al-Alimi, he was prime minister between 2018 and 2024 and a former negotiator with the Houthis.

He said: “The battle around Taiz is not just a battle for Taiz, but a broader battle that involves the whole of the western world, and one of the most important maritime straits. The Houthis know controlling Taiz is controlling the straits and it’s the highlands before the straits and the coastal city of Mocha and the Gulf of Aden. If Taiz is lost, access to the strait will be lost. The rest of the country will come later. The Houthi plan is to control the whole of Yemen.”

Taiz has become the new frontline in the war between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces after the Houthis launched a military campaign last month to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast, ending four years of relative calm in Yemen after a UN-brokered ceasefire froze the frontlines in 2022.

He said existing intelligence showed the Houthis were already seeking to control parts of the south, including the former Soviet camp at al-Sabiha, in the Lahij governorate, and eventually Aden. “The Houthis bleed a lot,” he said, “they suffer a lot, but they always want quickly to use their gains or any collapse to gain more land.”

With some Houthi leaders offering safe passage to armed groups to leave the city, he said for now the Houthis were allowing some fuel and commodities into the urban area of Taiz which houses more than 500,000 people, but in the meantime they were expanding their control of rural areas and smaller major cities.

Saeed said: “In a matter of days there will be a full siege and they will try to enter the city. I know the Houthis. They will show some flexibility until they are ready to control. It will be much worse than the siege of 2015. It will be catastrophic.”

He described Taiz as a modern democratic city untied to tribal culture, and predicted the Houthis would try to impose their Zaydi education, financial and tax systems very quickly, but the citizens would continue to resist. “The loss of Taiz would have a very significant symbolic impact on the idea of the modern state in Yemen and of resisting the Houthi project which relies on tribal networks and extremist religious education.”

blocks.caption: Displaced Yemeni families from al-Kadha, west of Taiz, at al-Akdaf refugee camp toward the end of last month. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP

blocks.text: Saeed admitted Taiz only had light weapons and the government had not been prepared for the loss of the west coast, allowing the Houthis to attack Taiz from four different axes.

“We have good troops,” he said, “but the problem is the coordination. We needed more communication between the National Shield Forces, National Resistance Forces and the Giants Brigades. It’s been a wake-up call inside the government and the army because not enough happened between the truce of 2022 and the restart of the fighting this year to reorganise the troops. The Houthi ideology solely is to fight.”

He added: “I hope now that the knife has come to our neck, and the Houthis represent a critical threat, the priority would be to come together to defeat the Houthis, and then to discuss other demands and guarantees.”

The exiled leader of the southern secessionist force, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, on Tuesday called for a mobilisation of southern troops against the Houthis, but coupled this with a demand for a referendum on secession within two years. He brought tens of thousands on to the streets in support on Wednesday, but his return would be a bitter pill for Riyadh to swallow.
Saeed said it was not a coincidence that the Houthi attack along the Red Sea coast in September had come when Iran was under heavy pressure.

“Its airplanes and airports cannot operate, 90% of the oil was coming out of Hormuz. That is why they attacked the Saudi east-to-west pipelines. The Houthis, by talking about a Saudi blockade, have found a reason to hit the Saudi oil installations, airports and they want to do it now because the only thing Iran can do is to keep expanding the consequences of the war for America.”

He said Houthi military capability and negotiating power had been transformed over the last decade leading to its ability to target key sites in Saudi Arabia now. “In 2017, the Houthis had nothing but blind missiles to fire at us that missed their targets.” By 2020, he said intelligence existed that Iranian experts operating from the Houthi capital Sana’a were training Houthis and in December of that year, in a devastatingly effective attack, they fired ballistic missiles at Aden airport. The attack left 28 dead and 107 injured, including Saeed himself, newly installed as prime minister. The missile travelled 186 miles (299km).

He explained: “We thought even then they did not have that many missiles, but since then the Iranians have expanded their manufacturing lines.” In January 2022, using missiles, the Houthis attacked Abu Dhabi oil tanker trucks more than 900 miles away.

In October 2022, inside Yemen, they struck the Nushayma oil terminal and al-Dhabba port, severely damaging government finances. By the time the US attacked Yemen in March 2025, he said “it was clear the Houthis had dozens of targeted missiles, land sea missiles and drones. They had become a unified front with Iran, and developed their missile base.”

He warned: “This is a new era of radical terrorism. It is not the old chaotic one of Isis and al-Qaida. It is semi-state actors and militias threatening powerful states with cheap technologies, and smuggled third-party components. The way Iran has invested in the Houthis could become a model for threatening navigation elsewhere. It is a new model of war, without traditional armies, needing different air defences. Gulf countries have to reshape and rethink their defences”.

articles.title: French police accused over war-like injuries to teenagers in school protests
articles.summary:
Four children allegedly ‘mutilated’ by explosive weapons and lawyers say unprecedented number held in custody

French lawyers and rights groups have said that several teenagers have suffered…

blocks.text: French lawyers and rights groups have said that several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons used during school protests, and an unprecedented number of children have been held in police custody, some of whom reported being hit or racially insulted.

France is in the fourth week of its biggest youth protest movement in decades, during which hundreds of high schools across the country have been blockaded as students demand the replacement of absent teachers and repairs to decrepit buildings.

Police have opened internal investigations into 36 allegations of officer violence against demonstrators, including four children allegedly being “mutilated” by explosive weapons, and six sustaining “significant injuries”, as well as other complaints over physical blows, insults or alleged sexual assault, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, told the senate.

Evan, a 15-year-old studying carpentry at a vocational high school, had a hand blown off in the explosion of a police stun grenade outside a school protest in Lens, northern France, on 5 October. His lawyer, Bertrand Wattez, said: “His injuries resemble war injuries.”

Wattez said Evan had gone to school to attend class and discovered a protest under way. He said Evan had not taken part in violence and denied the Béthune state prosecutor’s assertion that the grenade had been picked up from the ground. When the grenade exploded, Evan lost his left hand, several fingers from his right hand and suffered injuries to other parts of his body. He remained in hospital “in a very difficult condition” and his family had filed a criminal complaint, Wattez said.

Another boy, Eden, 14 – who had been near a school protest in Saint-Ouen-l’Aumône, north-west of Paris – suffered extensive facial injuries, including two fractures to his jaw, the loss of his bottom teeth and all his top teeth broken after he was allegedly hit by a shot from a grenade launcher.

His lawyer, Elsa Marcel, said the shot from a grenade launcher was fired at close range, from a distance of 1.5 metres. “This is the equivalent of war weaponry,” she said. The family has filed a legal complaint for attempted murder.

Eden’s parents said he had gone to school but found it blockaded and had wanted to go home. Video footage appeared to show him facing three riot police officers. One officer hit out in his direction with a truncheon and Eden kicked in the direction of the police before a grenade shot was fired. An officer has been suspended and placed under official investigation.

blocks.caption: Protesters take part in a demonstration in Paris.  Photograph: Firas Abdullah/EPA

blocks.text: This week, a police officer in the western city of Tours was charged with aggravated battery after Maël, a 16-year-old at a vocational high school, lost the use of his eye allegedly after a shot from a form of rubber-bullet launcher. The officer denies the charges. The family’s lawyer said Maël had not been involved in any violent confrontation with police but had simply been present at a school protest, and that the family felt a sense of “injustice”.

For several years, France has faced scrutiny over police use of explosive weapons, particularly after serious injuries were reported during the 2018-2019 gilets jaunes (yellow vests) street demonstrations, including allegations that people had lost eyes and had their hands and feet mutilated.

The current wave of protests has also led to lawyers raising concerns that an unprecedented number of children have been arrested and placed in police custody, with some lawyers reporting that teenagers said they were hit, humiliated or verbally abused during arrests.

Since the school protests began in mid-September, a total of 6,773 under-18s have been taken into police custody after they were arrested, the justice ministry said. For more than 1,000 of those children, no charges were brought; 2,190 are facing legal action and almost 2,000 were handed an alternative to further legal action, such as a citizenship course, without their case being heard at trial and without a conviction.
Lawyers said accusations against children included gathering with violent intent, violence against police and damage to property.

Nathalie Tehio, a lawyer and the president of the French Human Rights League, said the fact that only a minority of children’s cases would end up before a judge raised concerns that arrests could be unfounded. She said: “There are a record number of arrests … Often, the legal dossiers are empty. In reality, this is more about stopping people from demonstrating. I think there is a sense of hitting hard to try to dissuade people and scare them.”
Tehio said: “We have received accounts of racist comments made. Lawyers have told us that their clients say they have been humiliated or treated violently or pushed.”

Romain Boulet, a co-president of France’s Association of Criminal Lawyers, said: “Criminal lawyers are worried and raising concerns about the potential misuse of police powers to dissuade citizens aged under 18 from demonstrating.”

Mohamed Jaite, the president of the Paris branch of the leftwing union Syndicat des Avocats de France, has represented several teenagers stopped in Paris and its suburbs. “I have seen one youth limping in a police station,” he said. “Some have reported being humiliated or receiving racist and sexist insults.”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: High school students and union members march in Montpellier, in southern France. Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPA

blocks.text: Prisca Ancion, a lawyer from the leftwing lawyers’ group Collectif d’Action Judiciaire, which demonstrated this week in front of a high school in Saint-Denis, in the northern suburbs of Paris, said: “There have been racist insults during arrests, as well as homophobic, sexist comments or sexual touching. We encourage families to file complaints.”
Another lawyer from the collective, Romane Bartoli, who assisted several teenagers after their arrest, said: “Youngsters told us they were slapped, kicked or punched.”

One 16-year-old from a high school in a suburb north of Paris described being arrested 100 metres from his school on the day of a blockade in late September. He plans to study medicine at university and said he had intended to go to class before he saw there was a protest.
Answering questions from the Guardian with his lawyer, he said he had been held in police custody for more than 12 hours, mostly with two others in a police cell with two mattresses.
“It was hard psychologically because I felt I hadn’t done anything wrong,” he said. “I was hit with a truncheon and punched.”

He said a police officer told him to “shut his mouth” and said: “It’s always you lot,” which he understood to be a racist insult. He was released after a state prosecutor instructed him to carry out a citizenship course as an alternative to facing legal action.
The justice ministry and the interior ministry, which oversees policing, did not comment on allegations of insults or violence in police custody.
In parliament, Nuñez denied any form of excessive policing or police repression. He suspended the use of stun grenades at school demonstrations.

Audrey Bailleul, a magistrate and national representative of the Union Syndicale des Magistrats, said it was hard to have a clear view of events at this stage. She said: “There is nothing to show that there has voluntarily been a massive intention to not respect [legal] procedure.”

articles.title: Sydney suburb in lockdown as police search for man seen with shotgun
articles.summary:
Widespread manhunt in Dulwich Hill after man reportedly seen carrying longarm weapon

  • Get our breaking news…

blocks.text: A large swathe of Dulwich Hill in Sydney’s inner west has been locked down by police as they search for a man reportedly carrying a shotgun who allegedly set alight a stolen car in the area before fleeing on foot.
A police helicopter and armed tactical police focused their search for the man on an area around Williams Parade and Constitution Road.

Police were called to a car park on Williams Parade at about 10.20am on Friday in response to reports of a stolen vehicle. Officers were told a man carrying a longarm weapon was sitting inside the vehicle. It is alleged the man then set the car alight before fleeing on foot.
Speaking to reporters, police Supt Despa Fitzgerald said: “Do not approach this person – we understand he’s armed with a shotgun.”
She said there was no indication shots had been fired.

Police described the man as being of Caucasian appearance, aged in his 20s, about 160cm tall and of thin build, with shaggy hair. He was last seen on Union Street wearing a blue T-shirt and long black pants.
No injuries have been reported. Police have been doorknocking, telling residents to stay inside.
Light rail services in the area have been suspended and nearby businesses and cafes have been put into lockdown, along with neighbouring primary schools.
People outside the police exclusion zone are being advised to avoid the area.
More details soon …

articles.title: [OPINION] The weakest link may not be the subsea cables
articles.summary: Keeping the system resilient cannot be treated as the work of the Coast Guard or Navy alone. It also requires action from regulators, agencies, and operators.

blocks.text: Subsea cables entered the Philippine news twice in the span of a week, for different reasons.

The first involved a research vessel holding position in waters that host cable corridors connecting the country to Northeast Asia. On September 28, the Philippine Coast Guard reported that the vessel did not answer radio challenges and had displayed a physically impossible Automatic Identification System trail. It later deployed a ship and aircraft, disrupted what it described as unauthorized marine scientific research, and compelled the vessel to leave its position.
The second was a network disruption.

On October 2, the C2C Philippines-Singapore link went down while its Hong Kong link was under maintenance. Providers rerouted traffic, but the disruption coincided with reports of slow or intermittent connections. The Singapore link was restored the following day. Its cause had not been made public as of writing.

No public reporting has established a connection between the incidents. They should not be treated as one chain of events. But each exposes a different part of the same problem: what can the country detect and protect, what disruption can the network absorb? They also raise a third question that becomes critical when redundancy is no longer enough: how quickly can the system recover?
Taken together, this is a question of resilience.
For the Philippines, subsea cable resilience is a question of archipelagic governance.

This is the approach being explored by The Asia Foundation through its Archipelagic Governance for Subsea Cables (AGOS) initiative, which brings government and industry together to look at subsea cable resilience beyond the infrastructure itself. The cable is only one part of a wider system of infrastructure, institutions, policies, and capabilities. The system connects what happens at sea with what happens on land.

For an archipelago, these connections are shaped by geography. Connectivity crosses maritime spaces, lands in different communities and jurisdictions, and depends on institutions and infrastructure spread across islands.

A disruption at sea can affect banking, government services, businesses, and emergency communications. Suspicious activity near a cable route may force government to respond before it fully understands the risk. Delays in maritime access can also delay repair and restoration.

The connection works both ways. Decisions on permits, power supply, security arrangements, and coordination with local governments affect whether the system can expand, remain operational, and recover from disruption.

The system stretches from cables on the seabed to landing stations and land-based networks. It also includes power, network operations, repair capacity, government policies, emergency arrangements, and the institutions responsible for them.

This makes protecting cables and building cable resilience related but different tasks. Protecting a cable is about reducing the risk of damage or interference. Resilience is about whether the larger system can continue to function when disruption happens.

Across AGOS consultations with government and industryparticipants spoke about resilience in different ways: protecting the system, keeping services running during a disruption, and restoring connectivity quickly. Taken together, their inputs pointed to three qualities describing a resilient system: protected, adaptable, and recoverable. These qualities do not come from infrastructure alone. They also depend on the policies, capabilities, and coordination that allow the system to function.

A protected system can identify and manage risks. An adaptable system can reroute traffic and keep essential services running. A recoverable system can quickly mobilize maritime access, repair permits, security, technical teams, and local support.
The cable alone can do none of these things.

The question, then, is not only whether the Philippines can prevent something from happening to a cable. Not every cable fault, anchor drag, natural hazard, technical failure, or deliberate act can be prevented. The question is also whether the system around the cables can continue functioning when something does happen.

This is why keeping the system resilient cannot be treated as the work of the Coast Guard or Navy alone. Maritime authorities have distinct responsibilities at sea. But building a resilient subsea cables system also requires action from telecommunications regulators, economic and security agencies, emergency authorities, and operators.

Uncertainty over the cause of disruption further complicates the response. An incident may be accidental or deliberate, and establishing which takes time. But the response cannot wait for attribution. If services on land are already affected, continuity measures, repairs, and coordination have to kick in.

Attribution and resilience therefore operate on different clocks. Authorities may still be determining what happened while operators and government already need to keep services running and preparing for recovery.

The Philippines already has laws, mandates, and mechanisms that cover parts of the system. Telecommunications and data-transmission rules govern networks. Maritime authorities operate under their respective mandates at sea. Disaster-response mechanisms can support continuity. The Konektadong Pinoy Act provides an open-access framework for data transmission, while Executive Order No. 32 streamlines permitting process for telecommunications and internet infrastructure.
The challenge is not always the lack of a policy. It is whether existing mandates can be brought together quickly enough when an incident crosses institutional boundaries.

Which agency receives the first report? What threshold triggers interagency coordination? Who verifies the incident, secures the area, prioritizes essential services, authorizes emergency access, and communicates with affected communities? Which approvals can be expedited, and under whose authority? What information should operators share with government, and what information should remain protected?
An incident protocol is one way to answer those questions before a disruption. It should connect detection to assessment, protection, continuity, repair, and public communication.

This is where an archipelagic approach becomes operational rather than conceptual. The task is not necessarily to create another institution. The task is to make sure the institutions that already hold different parts of the system know when and how to act together.

The Philippines is not starting from scratch. PCG detected and acted on unusual vessel activity. Operators shifted traffic when an international route became unavailable. Companies already invest in additional capacity, route diversity, and repair arrangements.

At the September 29 AGOS Forum, PLDT Global Corporation President and CEO, Albert Villa-Real put the industry case plainly: “Capacity without diversity is not resilience.” He also pointed to exploratory discussions among Philippine operators on shared or complementary infrastructure that could provide greater redundancy.

Route diversity makes the network more adaptable, but redundancy does not address the whole resilience problem.When redundancy is no longer enough, or when physical repair is required, maritime access, government processes, security, information sharing, and repair capacity become part of the system’s ability to recover.

Those efforts show that competition and cooperation can coexist. No single operator or government agency controls all the elements needed for resilience. Some forms of cooperation are therefore necessary, and possible, even within a competitive industry.

What is needed is a clearer way for the different parts of the system to work together. That means having a common operating picture that protects sensitive information, clear rules on when to share it, an agreed response protocol, and a process for settling government requirements before a repair vessel is ready to move.

International experience shows a growing recognition that protecting undersea infrastructure requires cooperation between government and industry. After several incidents involving damaged cables in the Baltic Sea, NATO launched Baltic Sentry to strengthen surveillance and support national authorities. NATO also works with industry through its Critical Undersea Infrastructure Network.
But the Philippines cannot simply copy the Baltic model.

Archipelagic governance must respond to the country’s own geography, institutions, communities, and risks. It does not require placing every decision under one institution. Nor does it mean treating subsea cables primarily as a military or security problem. It requires each institution to understand how its authority connects with others, what actions should follow when an incident occurs, and how consequences at sea will be managed on land.

The recent incidents point to a broader lesson. A country can patrol the waters above a cable and still lack resilience. It can add cable capacity and still lack resilience. It can have repair arrangements, permits, emergency authorities, and capable institutions, but still find that these pieces do not connect quickly enough when disruption occurs.
For an archipelago, the weakest link may therefore not be the cable itself. It may be the system around it. – Rappler.com

Kat Tolosa is director of The Asia Foundation’s Governance and Resilience unit in the Philippines. Taj Basman is a program officer in the same unit and leads the Foundation’s Archipelagic Governance for Subsea Cables initiative. The views expressed are their own.

articles.title: Sara Duterte on NBI's Matibag: 'I'm not interested in him, he's a nobody'
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte called National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag a "nobody" amid the agency's investigation into the properties linked to her and her family.

blocks.text: Published October 16, 2026 11:29am
Vice President Sara Duterte called National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag a "nobody" amid the agency's investigation into the properties linked to her and her family.

"Hindi ako interesado sa kanya. Walang interested kay Atty. Matibag. He's a nobody," Duterte said in an ambush interview in Zamboanga City, when asked for a comment on the NBI chief's challenge to file a case if she thinks he is biased or doing something wrong.
(I'm not interested in him. No one is interested in Atty. Matibag. He's a nobody.)
GMA News Online reached out to Matibag for a comment, but he has yet to respond as of posting time.

The NBI on Tuesday referred its fact-finding investigation report on the vice president's Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) to the Office of the Ombudsman for evaluation and appropriate action.
The investigation compared the vice president's SALN in 2024-2025 to the certified true copies of land titles obtained from the Land Registration Authority (LRA).
Duterte said she will give her explanation on the NBI findings to the Office of the Ombudsman.

"'Yung regarding sa Statement of Assets and Liabilities ko, it is already a subject in the impeachment. At sinubmit na rin 'yun sa Ombudsman. So ito 'yung mga proper forum kung saan mas makakabuti doon kami magbigay ng aming sagot at explenasyon. Kaysa sa makipagsagutan tayo kay Atty. Matibag na nakita naman natin na mali-mali 'yung mga sinasabi," she said.

(Regarding my statements of assets and liabilities, these are already a subject of the impeachment proceedings. They were also submitted to the Ombudsman. These are the proper forums where it would be best for us to provide our response and explanation—rather than responding to Atty. Matibag, whose statements, as we have seen, are riddled with errors.)
'Political persecution'
Meanwhile, Atty. Paolo Panelo Jr., spokesperson for the vice president, said Duterte declared all her assets and liabilities in her SALN "correctly and in good faith."

"The series of press conferences by NBI Director Melvin Matibag on supposed discrepancies in properties declared in the Vice President's SALN is just the latest example of the Marcos administration's weaponization of government institutions for political persecution," Panelo said in a statement.

"The Vice President maintains that she declared all her assets and liabilities in her SALN correctly and in good faith, and all allegations to the contrary are false. She is confident this will be proven in the impeachment trial, and if necessary, before the Ombudsman once given formal notice," he added.
The Office of the Ombudsman has vowed to conduct an impartial probe on the NBI's referral on alleged missing declarations of the Vice President in her SALN.

The NBI is also investigating the accounts of dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., a former member of the security detail of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco, who alleged that he delivered suitcases containing cash to the vice president, former president Rodrigo Duterte, and Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo "Pulong" Duterte on Velasco's instructions.
Gracioso estimated that he had delivered more than P2 billion to Sara Duterte.
Matibag has said the bureau is investigating properties supposedly linked to the vice president and her family to follow a pattern that was established in Gracioso's affidavit.

The vice president, Congressman Duterte, and Velasco have denied the allegations. Velasco has insisted that the allegations have "no basis." Congressman Duterte, for his part, have dismissed Gracioso's claims as "pure fiction" and a "fairy-tale lie."
Panelo said Matibag aired the NBI findings publicly without previously informing the vice president and giving her an opportunity to respond.

"That is not the work of a fair and impartial investigative body. That is a shameless smear campaign against the Vice President using public funds, headlined by a man with a documented conflict of interest against her," Panelo said.
He also questioned why the NBI findings were excluded by the prosecution in the impeachment trial, where the defense could answer. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Firearms manufacturer standing for One Nation in NSW opposes post-Bondi gun laws that reclassify weapons
articles.summary:
Jeff Bacon, managing director of Oceania Precision, has been described by the NSW party’s leader as ‘my go-to man on the firearms industry’

A firearms manufacturer hoping to represent One…

blocks.text: A firearms manufacturer hoping to represent One Nation in New South Wales wants to repeal gun laws introduced following the Bondi beach massacre, after arguing “every single one” of the rifles he produces was banned in the state.
Earlier this month, One Nation’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, and the federal MP Barnaby Joyce revealed Jeff Bacon would be second on the party’s upper house ticket in the March state election.
Bacon is the managing director of Oceania Precision, a weapons manufacturer based in Tamworth.
The announcement of his candidacy was made in Tamworth before Bacon hosted a One Nation forum on firearms legislation attended by gun lobby groups and local gun clubs, as well as Newman and Joyce.

Newman said Bacon was “not only a firearms owner, but he is also a manufacturer and also he is an innovator” with “patents across the world”. He said Bacon would be “my go-to man on the firearms industry”.
Bacon ran as the lower house candidate for Tamworth with the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party in 2019. He joined the Nationals in 2023 before defecting to One Nation.
On 3 October this year, he said in Tamworth that running for parliament again “wasn’t a hard decision”.
“To be honest I’d rather continue in my business than be in some way forced to step into politics,” he said.
“[But] I’m going to do everything that I can do – not only to fight for the repeal of the legislation.”

In a statement at the time, Bacon said: “One Nation will repeal the firearms element of the Terrorism and Other Legislation Amendment Act, restoring rights to what they were when we had a functioning system before December last year, when the Minns government and the Liberal party rushed legislation through on Christmas Eve.”

In December 2025, Labor and the Liberals changed the law to limit recreational license-holders to four firearms and primary producers to 10, and legislated for NSW to participate in a joint buyback of weapons with the federal government. NSW is the only state to sign on to the federal scheme so far. It’s due to begin on 2 November.
The NSW parliament also voted to recategorise weapons including straight-pull and lever-release rifles meaning recreational hunters will no longer be able to own them.

One of the alleged Bondi shooters, Indian national Sajid Akram, owned six weapons on a recreational hunting licence, including straight-pull rifles allegedly used during the antisemitic attack on 14 December that killed 15 people during Hanukah celebrations.

Oceania Precision’s website describes its rifles as “built specifically for law enforcement”. It currently advertises one model: a select-fire tactical rifle which it describes as “restricted” for law enforcement.
As recently as June, it described itself as a manufacturer for the “Australian domestic and professional market”, according to website snapshots from the Internet Archive.

At that time, it advertised two models for the commercial market, the straight-pull SP25-TAC and the lever-release Renegade, although archived webpages suggest both have been described as “not available in NSW” since last year, before the firearms changes enacted after the Bondi shootings.

In January, Bacon told the Northern Daily Leader that the government’s firearms reforms had seen “every single one” of his rifles banned in NSW, the paper reported. He said his business would be “broke in six months if this continues – we’re done, we’re finished”.
“I’m in the middle of two manufacturing runs right now,” he said at the time.
“We’re on hold right now, we just don’t know what’s happening. We’ve had all of our orders cancelled.”
In August, Bacon told trade website Defence Connect that his business was at risk of collapse following the gun reforms.

“Our entire research and development budget is funded through our commercial sporting sales,” he said at the time. “These revenue streams have been severely impacted, significantly reducing our ability to invest in ongoing innovation and product development.”

The laws recategorising straight-pull and lever-release weapons have yet to take effect. Owners will be able to surrender them over a 12-month period under the buyback – after which they will become illegal for those on recreational licenses.
after newsletter promotion
One Nation is running on a platform of repealing the buyback and most changes to firearms laws in NSW since the Bondi attack.

After One Nation won the Farrer byelection in South Australia in May, the Oceania Precision Instagram account posted a picture of Bacon with the federal leader, Pauline Hanson. The caption stated: “The 2027 NSW state election is fast approaching, we need to support the people who support our industry, join the party today.”

In Tamworth in early October, Bacon said he supported changes voted through as part of December’s reforms which are set to make Australian citizenship a requirement for recreational firearms license after the buyback is complete.

“What happened at the end of last year was a tragedy but what followed was probably some of the worst politics that we’ve ever seen,” he said when launching his upper house tilt. Bacon said the weapons industry hadn’t been consulted.
He cited a survey by gun lobby group the Shooting Industry Foundation of Australia which suggested that half of the dealers in NSW were facing closure.

One Nation is polling at 25% of the primary vote in NSW, according to a Sydney Morning Herald Resolve poll in September. If that support eventuated in March, the party could win at least five upper house seats. The Coalition was on 24% in the Resolve poll.
The NSW Nationals voted against changes to firearms laws in December while the Liberal party supported them.

The opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, has walked back her support since then. The Liberal party announced last month that it would scrap caps for primary producers and freeze the buyback while an inquiry examined other changes.

The Resolve poll suggested that opposition to the gun reforms among One Nation voters – at 33% – was higher than for the other major parties. But a majority still supported the post-Bondi changes or were undecided.
The poll suggested 63% of all voters supported the reforms, slightly lower than after the attack, while 19% were opposed and the rest remained undecided.
Newman, speaking alongside Bacon earlier this month, said the firearms debate had become “a very sore point in the regions”.

Stephen Bendle, a senior advocacy adviser to the Alannah and Madeline Foundation, founded after the Port Arthur massacre, said attempts by One Nation or the Coalition to wind back the reforms was “outrageous politics that ignores the victims and survivors of Bondi and the expectations of the community”.
“The outrage is being led by commercial interests in the firearm industry. Mr Bacon and everyone else needs to understand that times change,” Bendle said.

“Many industries have to adapt to changing circumstances, whether they are government regulation or market forces. But in every case, the community determines what is in the community’s best interest.”
Bacon and One Nation did not respond when contacted for comment.

items: Forty-six members of the newly elected Bangsamoro Parliament signed a coalition agreement, backing interim Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua ahead of the October 30 vote for the region's leadership.

Macacua, supported by the Bangsamoro Federalist Party, is competing against Ahod Murad Ebrahim of the United Bangsamoro Justice Party, with both parties having a close electoral outcome in the September elections.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

DAVAO, Philippines – Forty-six members of the newly elected Bangsamoro Parliament signed a coalition agreement, giving interim Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua the backing of a majority ahead of the October 30 vote to choose the leader of the Muslim-majority region.

The coalition has more than the 41 votes needed for a majority in the 80-member Parliament, putting Macacua in a strong position to secure the top post, said Naguib Sinarimbo, a former Bangsamoro interior minister who was elected to represent a Cotabato City parliamentary district in September.

“We have more than the simple majority needed,” Sinarimbo told Rappler on Friday, October 16, adding that this ensures that Macacua would become the first elected chief minister of the seven-year-old Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.

blocks.caption: Who will be BARMM’s first elected chief minister?

blocks.text: Macacua, former commander of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front’s armed wing, is vying for the position against his former leader, Ahod “Al Haj” Murad Ebrahim, a former interim chief minister and the MILF’s chairman.

Macacua is backed by the months-old Bangsamoro Federalist Party, while Murad is supported by the MILF’s United Bangsamoro Justice Party. The two parties finished in a statistical tie in the September 14 parliamentary elections, with Macacua’s party winning 31 seats against 30 for the UBJP.
The remaining seats went to other political parties and sectoral representatives.
The newly elected Parliament is scheduled to convene for the first time on October 30, when its members will choose the first elected chief minister of the BARMM.

blocks.caption: IN NUMBERS: BARMM’s first elected parliament

blocks.text: On Thursday, October 15, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. welcomed the announcement of a 46-member majority coalition in the BARMM Parliament even as he reaffirmed the national government’s respect for the region’s autonomy.
In a statement, Marcos called the first-ever BARMM parliamentary elections in September as a “historic milestone” in the region’s pursuit of self-governance and lasting peace.

He said the national government recognizes the coalition’s formation and its intention to constitute the regional government through parliamentary processes, adding that it respected Parliament’s authority to choose its leadership under the Bangsamoro Organic Law.
Marcos said the national government was looking forward to working with the government formed by Parliament to promote peace, stability and inclusive development.

Macacua announced the signing of the coalition agreement during a gathering of newly elected parliament members in Davao City on Wednesday, October 14, even as he emphasized the need for unity to build a free, effective and stable Bangsamoro government. He also called on other groups and parties to respect the members’ decision.
The Macacua-led BFP spearheaded the coalition, which includes representatives of political parties, local governments, ethnolinguistic groups and former revolutionary organizations in BARMM.
Macacua said the formation of the “Government of the Day” would center on the selection and election of the chief minister.

“We will reach out our hands, we will heal divisions, and we will build a government that serves everyone,” Macacua said as he thanked those who joined the coalition for their trust, as well as the national government for respecting BARMM’s autonomy.
Lanao del Sur Governor Mamintal Adiong Jr., secretary-general of the Bangsamoro Grand Coalition (BGC), said the alliance aimed to sustain the peace process and achieve lasting peace in BARMM.

Adiong said the group had asked Marcos in Malacañang to continue the decommissioning program before the end of his term, with the aim of securing a final exit agreement between the MILF and the national government.
He said the BGC was open to dialogue with other parties, including the UBJP and the BFP, to advance Marcos’ call for unity in the region’s leadership.
“Who wouldn’t want peace? We all aspire for that, which is why we have an autonomous region for Muslims. So hopefully, lasting peace will be achieved,” Adiong said.

Coalition leaders also held a strategic planning workshop in Davao City to set legislative and executive priorities for the regular parliament’s first 100 days and five years. Some UBJP members came to participate.
BARMM Interior Minister Jordan Bayam said the elected parliament faces higher expectations than the interim Bangsamoro Transition Authority.
“This time, this is not just a BTA, but this is an elected parliament. So the task and the expectations of our people is so high,” Bayam said, stressing the need for unity around a common agenda.
Lampa Pandi, a parliament member-elect representing Lanao del Sur’s fourth district under the UBJP, said he attended to support a long-term direction for the region beyond partisan politics.

“I am not playing politics here, it’s more of the direction of the parliament where we aim to unite for the good of Bangsamoro,” Pandi said. He was joined by Tawakal Midting, who won in Maguindanao del Sur’s first parliamentary district. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: The Philippine leader says Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan's remark 'deserves a discussion between the ambassador and myself;

The Philippine leader says Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan's remark 'deserves a discussion between the ambassador and myself;

items: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. plans to summon Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan due to remarks perceived as a threat regarding the use of force in tensions between the Philippines and China.

The Department of Foreign Affairs criticized Jing's comments as a poor choice of words that implied a threat, while the Chinese embassy accused the DFA of misinterpretation and undermining diplomatic relations.
Tensions between the Philippines and China have escalated recently, with ongoing maritime confrontations and political pressures, including sanctions from Beijing against Philippine officials.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will summon Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan over a “threat” the envoy had made on the use of force in dealing with tensions between Manila and Beijing.

Asked in a chance interview if he would summon Jing over his remark, Marcos said in a chance interview on the sidelines of the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) anniversary celebration, “I think that deserves a discussion between the ambassador and myself.”
A summon, especially one made by the head of state, is among the highest means of communication a government can use to express concern, disapproval, or anger to an ambassador’s home office.

Should the summon push through, it would be the second time for Marcos to summon Jing to the Palace in just over 10 months of being posted in Manila. The last time was in July, after a Filipino soldier was injured in a violent confrontation with China Coast Guard (CCG) personnel in Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal in the West Philippine Sea.

Echoing the view of the Department of Foreign Affairs, Marcos said of Jing’s remark on Friday: “Well it sounds very much to me like a threat, and it is not a very diplomatic statement to be made. So we perhaps would like to understand what exactly it is that he means.”
In an interview with reporters on October 15, Jing insisted that China was no troublemaker in the region and blamed some Philippine officials for causing tensions between Manila and Beijing.

The veteran diplomat, who was assigned to the United States before being sent to the Philippines in December 2025, added: “We should feel fortunate enough that you have a neighbor like China in this region. If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we’ll not use force. We love peace.”
The DFA, in a statement late October 15, criticized Jing for his “poor choice of words that would seem to convey a thinly veiled threat of the use of force.”

The Chinese embassy has since hit back through an October 16 statement, accusing the DFA of “selective quotation and overinterpretation” and said “diplomacy must be honest and straightforward in order to reduce misunderstandings and prevent misjudgments.”

It also claimed that “certain individuals are actively seeking to undermine normal exchanges and cooperation between the two countries” and that the DFA should “play a more responsible role in preventing such actions.” The embassy has made similar statements in the past.

Tense public exchanges between the Chinese embassy and Philippine government agencies — the DFA included, albeit rarely — have been a recurring feature in bilateral ties of the two countries, despite Marcos saying that he wants a “reset” in bilateral relations. The rhetoric is matched by maritime tensions and confrontations across different parts of the Philippines — from northern areas close to Batanes and westward in the West Philippine Sea.

Political pressure has also escalated between the two countries. Beijing sanctioned Teodoro and his family over his remarks against Beijing, including calling it unreliable in the context of South China Sea code negotiations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which Manila chairs.

Most recently, tensions have been spurred by statements by impeached Vice President Sara Duterte who is accused to have recieved millions from China state-owned firms through businesses linked to her and her husband. In retaliation, Duterte said the Philippines is seen as a “troublemaker” in the region over tensions with China — over the West Philippine Sea, and even over scrutiny when it comes to business ties with the Asian superpower.

“Troublemaker” is how Beijing has characterized Manila in the past whenever maritime tensions rise in the West Philippine Sea, an area that includes the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone in the South China Sea. China claims almost all of the South China Sea, despite a 2016 Arbitral Award finding the suppose historical claim baseless. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Marcos: Chinese ambassador's force remark ‘sounds very much like a threat’
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said on Friday, October 16, that Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan’s remark about China’s ability to use force “sounds very much like a threat and not a…

blocks.text: October 16, 2026 | 10:33am

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said on Friday, October 16, that Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan’s remark about China’s ability to use force “sounds very much like a threat and not a diplomatic statement to be made.”

Marcos told reporters the government would like to understand “what it is exactly he means.” Asked if he would summon the envoy, the president said: “It deserves a discussion between the ambassador and myself.”

The president weighed in after the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), late Thursday, October 15, rebuked Jing for a “poor choice of words” that it said seemed to convey “a thinly veiled threat of the use of force.” The department asked diplomats in Manila to watch their language.

“The business of diplomacy requires tact and restraint in order to create space necessary for discourse, dialogue and engagement, regardless of the disparity in positions or perspectives,” the DFA said in a statement released late Thursday, October 15. It called the remark “hardly helpful” given the “complicated bilateral ties” between the two countries.
Such language risks further eroding “mutual trust and confidence," the DFA added.
Jing uttered the remarks in question to reporters on Thursday on the sidelines of the second Diliman Dialogues, organized by the Philippines-China Studies Center of Diliman College in Quezon City.
Rejecting the "troublemaker" tag for China, Jing said: "If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not use force. You know, we love peace."

“Who is the troublemaker?” the Chinese diplomat asked. He cited efforts to “go after” Chinese teachers, the use of the army to arrest “innocent” Chinese workers, and daily “smear” attacks that he said were meant to incite hatred between the two countries. He said the Philippines “should feel fortunate” to have a neighbor like China in the region.
The exchange is the latest public clash between the Philippines and the Chinese Embassy since Jing arrived in Manila in December 2025.

In January, the department made firm representations to Jing over the embassy’s increasingly combative social media posts targeting senators. Since then, there has not been a let-up in the tone and frequency of the embassy's public criticisms of Philippine officials expressing disagreement with Beijing's stance on the 2016 arbitral ruling and Manila's sea rights, among others.
'Selective quotation'
The embassy on Friday morning publicly responded to the DFA and argued its ambassador was the subject of "selective quotation." It said the DFA's admonishment was "regrettable."

“This kind of selective quotation and overinterpretation demonstrates that there is still a long way to go in fostering effective communication and dialogue between China and the Philippines,” the embassy said in a statement.

The embassy said relations were at “an extremely sensitive stage” and that “certain individuals,” whom it did not name, were trying to undermine exchanges between the two countries. It urged the DFA to “play a more responsible role” in preventing such actions.
Jing’s remarks on teachers appeared to refer to the recent withdrawal of about 150 Chinese volunteer teachers from Chinese-language schools.

The Federation of Filipino Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry Inc. said the teachers were recalled at their parents’ request, with the approval of the federation and the embassy, after reports by Ray Powell of the monitoring group SeaLight raised suspicions about Chinese-language schools in the country.

The Chinese ambassador did not specify which worker arrests he meant, but Philippine authorities have detained hundreds of Chinese workers this year in raids targeting suspected human trafficking and illegal online gambling. The embassy has singled out a May raid on a steel plant in Misamis Oriental, insisting the Chinese workers held there had valid permits and blaming Teodoro for sending in the military to join the arrest.

Jing himself has warned that Manila faces a greater risk of confrontation unless direct military-to-military communication with Beijing, suspended by Teodoro, is restored. On October 12, the embassy accused Teodoro of shutting down those channels for “political self interests.”

The Armed Forces of the Philippines has backed Teodoro's action, saying this "direct communications has been used as a smokescreen by the Chinese Communist Party to perpetuate their illegal presence, coercive and aggressive actions and deceptive messaging not only on our maritime domain but even on land."

articles.title: Evacuations issued as multiple wildfires ignite in hot, windy California
articles.summary:
Largest blaze the Henderson fire near San Diego as strong winds and severe heat could fuel rapid spread

Multiple wildfires ignited across California on Thursday as the state braced for more…

blocks.text: Multiple wildfires ignited across California on Thursday as the state braced for more strong winds and high temperatures that could fuel rapid fire growth over the next several days.

The largest blaze, dubbed the Henderson fire, erupted in Camp Pendleton, a San Diego Marine Corps training base, and quickly consumed more than 1,000 acres. Evacuations have been issued and officials briefly closed part of the Interstate 5, a major highway in the region.
Videos of the incident shared by the California department of forestry and fire protection showed a wall of flames and thick, black smoke that thrashed in the strong winds alongside the highway.

Along with the Henderson fire, which was 0% contained by 6pm on Thursday, evacuation warnings were issued for two brush fires in the Los Angeles area: one in Azusa, a city near the San Gabriel mountains north-east of Los Angeles, and another in Malibu.

The blazes broke out during high wind event that has increased fire risks across southern California. The so-called Santa Ana winds will linger through Saturday, according to the National Weather Service, and the potential for extreme fire behavior and rapid spread could still rise.

“A moderate to strong Santa Ana wind will bring widespread strong winds and critical fire weather conditions to much of south-west California,” the National Weather Service said in a forecast issued on Thursday.

Strong, dry winds could reach 20-40mph (32 to 64 km/h), with gusts from 50-70mph in the San Gabriel mountains in Los Angeles county and the Santa Susana mountains, which are mostly in Ventura county, officials said. Critical fire weather conditions are also forecast for portions of the Santa Lucia mountains in San Luis Obispo county.
The elevated risks come amid a tumultuous start to autumn that has already brought severe heatwaves, high surf and flooding – and this may just be the beginning, according to experts.

Destructive conditions fueled by a potentially historic El Niño brewing in the Pacific will continue to mount through the end of this year and into next. The impacts, which have already raised sea levels, increased temperatures and supercharged storms in the Pacific, layer on top of natural hazards and those fueled by the human-caused climate crisis.

blocks.caption: Water is dropped on the Peak fire by helicopter on Thursday in Azusa, California.  Photograph: Jae C Hong/AP

blocks.text: The Santa Ana winds in this week’s forecast are expected during this time of year, along with higher fire dangers that typically linger in the state through November. But on the heels of the recent storm surge that battered the California coast, the weather whiplash has left residents reeling.

With the threat of fire, heat and sea level rise colliding, as the state readies for more incoming effects from El Niño, Kevin McGowan, the director of LA’s office of emergency management, urged residents to be ready. “People should continue to prepare not just for one hazard,” he said during a recent briefing, “but all hazards”.
In Los Angeles, where strong Santa Ana winds fueled the devastating 2025 firestorm that killed more than 30 people, the warnings were sharply felt.

While this event is nowhere near the magnitude of the one that tore through communities across the county in 2025, neighborhoods are still being rebuilt after multiple blazes consumed more than 16,000 structures.Huge burn scars left behind have increased the dangers for debris flows and landslides, should the elevated chances of severe storms materialize over this winter.
Officials are preparing to meet the fire risks head on to protect communities now and in months that follow. New fires will mean more risks in the season ahead.

“If there is any significant fire activity this week, it would be somewhat poorly timed in the context of El Niño,” said climate scientist Daniel Swain in an online briefing on Wednesday. “We know the likelihood of a wet winter in southern California is now very high. [Fire] would further raise the stakes.”
The Peak fire in Azusa ignited around 1pm and grew to 43 acres in just two hours. Firefighters have mostly wrangled the blaze, enabling local mandatory evacuations to be downgraded to warnings.
The Bryson fire in Malibu was roughly 80 acres by 6pm and embers were being carried by the winds, fueling the blaze’s spread, LA fire officials told the Los Angeles Times.
Thousands of people in California were also without electricity on Thursday as utilities tried to reduce the risk of hot, windy weather that could blow over power lines and spark wildfires.

In northern California, nearly 62,000 customers in 26 counties had no electricity, according to Pacific Gas and Electric Company. The company began proactively turning off power on Wednesday night. Weather conditions that increase the fire risk were expected to last through Saturday.
Los Angeles Fire chief, Jaime Moore, said staffing has been augmented and equipment pre-deployed so crews will be ready.
“We are asking residents to do their part too,” he added. “Clear the streets, have a plan and stay informed.”

With the risks rising across California, the state’s office of emergency services has also increased its coordination and readied resources to support local officials should disaster strike, according to spokesperson Chris Dargan.
The National Weather Service issued fire weather warnings for parts of central and northern California, starting on Thursday and lasting through Friday morning, saying any fires would spread rapidly.
“It’s a pretty widespread event of elevated fire weather, so the whole SoCal region should really be on alert,” said Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.
The Associated Press contributed in reporting

articles.title: FBI investigates letters with ‘unknown substance’ sent to US election officials
articles.summary:
Election officers in Louisiana and Oklahoma receive a powdery substance, prompting evacuations

The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service are investigating letters sent to state officials…

blocks.text: The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service are investigating letters sent to state officials and election offices across the country containing an “unknown substance”.

Just weeks before November’s US midterm elections, election officers in Louisiana and Oklahoma received envelopes containing a powdery substance, leading to evacuations. A similar package containing white powder was also sent to the Ohio secretary of state, but the US Postal Service intercepted the package.

Later on Thursday, the office of Arizona’s secretary of state received a similar envelope that was opened by staff, prompting hazmat and law enforcement response as well as evacuations at the state capitol.

“This is a sobering moment that highlights the reality of election administration in this country today,” Arizona secretary of state Adrian Fontes said in a statement. Police told 12News there were no injuries reported, and an investigation is under way.

The US Senate sergeant at arms, who serves as chief law enforcement for the Senate, informed members of the upper chamber on Thursday of the investigation in a message, obtained by the Associated Press.

The notice said law enforcement officials were working to intercept additional mail, but it is possible some could reach their destination. Federal authorities have urged recipients to treat the mail as “potentially hazardous”.

Brendan Donahue, a senior official with the US Postal Inspection Service, confirmed the investigation into the suspicious mailings during a press conference on Thursday. “We are committed to protecting our nation’s election officials from threatening and dangerous mail. Any threat or attack on an election official is unacceptable,” Donahue said.
The US Postal Inspection Service referred the Guardian to the FBI.

In a statement, the FBI said it would not confirm specific instances but said that it was “investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State office and their related election officers” alongside the US Postal Inspection Service.

“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” the FBI said. “We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.”
The FBI declined to comment on what the purported substance may have been.
In Oklahoma, state troopers determined the substance mailed to the Oklahoma state capitol complex was non-hazardous.

In Cook county, Illinois, an envelope containing only white powder was sent to Maria Pappas, the treasurer, on Thursday morning, prompting a response from local emergency responders and law enforcement.
The powder turned out to be baking powder, Pappas’s office confirmed to the Guardian.

“Unfortunately, one-tenth of 1% of the population causes 100% of the problems: crimes, threats, murders, beatings and abusiveness, etc. Too bad that normal folk have to have their guard up when a minority of folk lash out with their craziness,” Pappas said in a statement.
Another letter containing an unknown substance was sent to the Pennsylvania state department but intercepted by the USPS, Votebeat reported Thursday.
Two organizations representing secretaries of state and state election directors released a joint statement raising alarm at the mail containing the unknown substance.

The National Association of Secretaries of State (NASS) and National Association of State Election Directors (NASED) “are deeply concerned by these incidents”, the organizations wrote in a statement on Wednesday.

“As we have each stated in the past, threats against election officials and workers have no place in our democracy,” they wrote. “Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties.”
Other officials have received mail containing suspicious substances, including Chris Murphy, the Democratic senator from Connecticut. The letter was sent to his Hartford office, according to NBC.
Alex Padilla, the senator from California, was also the target of a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted by the USPS.

Similar incidents have arisen during election cycles in the country. During the 2024 election, at least 14 election offices across the country had received mail containing white powder. In some cases, the substance turned out to be flour.
In 2023, election offices in six states also received mail containing white powder. In some cases, the powder contained trace amounts of fentanyl, a powerful opioid.
The Associated Press contributed reporting
