articles.title: 'It's really hard to believe' - How Oregon primary school shooting unfolded
articles.summary: Three children aged 5, 8 and 11 and a teacher were killed after a 16-year-old suspect opened fire in the city of Bend, local police say.

blocks.text: Four victims, including a teacher and three children aged 5, 8 and 11, were killed in a shooting at a primary school in the US state of Oregon, local police say.

A 16-year-old suspect forced his way into the school by firing at locked doors. He was also killed in the shooting by an armed member of the community who followed the suspect inside the school, police said at a press conference.
Two additional victims, a 7-year-old and another teacher, were hurt and transported to hospital in critical condition.

articles.title: Three children and a teacher killed by 16-year-old at Oregon primary school
articles.summary: A teen assailant was pursued into the school by an armed community member, who shot him dead, said police.

blocks.text: "We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy," Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said in a statement.
"No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing."
Local law enforcement responded to reports of an active shooter at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, at 12:59 local time, Bend Police Department spokeswoman Sheila Miller told reporters.
The first call indicated that an unknown suspect had shot into a car, she said. Photos released from the scene show a red truck with bullet holes.
Minutes later, the local county dispatch received a flood of 911 calls and law enforcement were sent to the scene.
The suspected shooter was shot dead at around 13:02pm, Miller said.
While police said the shooter was a local 16-year-old boy, they declined to add further details pending the ongoing investigation.

A 16-year-old shooter opened fire on Thursday, October 15, at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, killing four people, including three children, before being killed by an armed person who had pursued the assailant into the school, police said.
The shooter entered the school by shooting through locked doors, police said, without offering any details beyond the shooter’s age.

The dead were children aged 5, 8 and 11 and one teacher. In addition, a 7-year-old student and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to hospital with critical injuries, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told a press conference.

blocks.caption: RESPONSE. Emergency personnel direct traffic at the scene of a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, US, October 15, 2026. Reuters

blocks.text: Oregon Governor Tina Kotek, appearing at the same briefing, thanked the community member who “heroically intervened to stop further loss of life.”

“No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have to live through this kind of day, and as we learn more about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured, and their families and their loved ones, we are going to do a lot of crying, and we are going to cry together, and we’re probably going to cry privately,” Kotek said.
Krantz said the community member, whom he did not identify, had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him.
The shooting took place in Bend, a city of about 100,000 residents in rural central Oregon, 280 km southeast of Portland, in the Oregon high desert adjacent to the Deschutes National Forest.
Silver Rail Elementary School serves kindergarten through fifth grade, roughly ages 5 to 11, and has about 450 students and 40 staff members, officials said.
Police said they received a call around 1 pm (2000 GMT) that “indicated that an unknown man had shot into a car” at Silver Rail Elementary School.
Moments later, emergency dispatchers received multiple calls “reporting that a person had entered the school and begun shooting,” police said in a statement.
Officers arrived within three minutes and found that the suspect had been shot dead. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Shape of Pope Leo’s papacy more uncertain after cancer diagnosis
articles.summary: The world's 1.4 billion Catholics are again unexpectedly facing the reality of a sick pope

blocks.text: POPE LEO. Pope Leo XIV delivers his 'Urbi et Orbi' (To the city and the world) message from the main balcony of St. Peter's Basilica, on Easter Sunday, at the Vatican, April 5, 2026.
Vatican Media/­Handout via REUTERS
The world's 1.4 billion Catholics are again unexpectedly facing the reality of a sick pope

items: Pope Leo XIV, diagnosed with lung cancer after surgery, faces uncertainty regarding his health and papal duties.
His planned trip to South America, a high priority for him, may be postponed depending on his recovery.
The Vatican has been unusually transparent about Leo's health, with experts suggesting a potentially positive prognosis if the cancer is early-stage.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

VATICAN – When US Cardinal Robert Prevost emerged on the balcony of St. Peter’s Basilica in May 2025 as Pope Leo XIV, the new leader of the Catholic Church, he struck a stark contrast from his predecessor Francis.

Leo, young for a pope at 69 then, appeared energetic, spoke in a strong voice and had no known history of health issues. Francis, who died at 88, had become increasingly frail during his 12-year papacy.

With the Vatican’s announcement on Tuesday, October 13, that Leo, now 71, was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed part of his right lung that afternoon, the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics are again unexpectedly facing the reality of a sick pope.

blocks.caption: Pope Leo back on his feet after shock cancer diagnosis

blocks.text: Leo, the first US-born pontiff, has emerged as an increasingly influential voice beyond the Church, raising alarm about the risks posed by artificial intelligence and drawing the ire of US President Donald Trump by criticizing the Iran war.

The future shape of Leo’s papacy — once expected to be dynamic with many foreign trips and the pope stepping into a leading moral role on the global stage — is now more uncertain. Medical experts say the pope’s prognosis will depend on several factors, including whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes, currently unknown.
“It’s too early to say how this will affect Pope Leo’s agenda and his ability to carry on the duties of the papacy,” John Thavis, a Vatican expert and author, told Reuters.
“If his recovery is complete and no aggressive therapy is needed, the pope may be able to carry on as usual,” he said.

One immediate question Leo faces is whether to proceed with an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17. The trip is known to be a high priority for the pope, who spent decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru.

The original schedule, announced last month, would have made it one of the most intense foreign trips ever undertaken by a pope, with Leo leading some 50 events and giving 36 speeches across a 10-city tour.

Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital, said the trip may need to be postponed, depending on Leo’s recovery.
“A trip to South America that quickly is possible, if this is an early-stage lung cancer and no further therapy is needed, but it is a tight timeline, and recovery is highly variable,” said Liu.

blocks.caption: What is lung adenocarcinoma, the cancer diagnosed in Pope Leo?

blocks.text: Leo had been keeping a rapid pace of foreign travel, already making four tours in 2026 and attracting large crowds. More than 800,000 people turned out to see him in Paris last month.

Catholics have often witnessed a pope deal with illness. Francis, who had part of one lung removed as a young adult, was prone to respiratory infections. He was also hospitalized as pope for colon and hernia surgeries.
John Paul II began to suffer symptoms of Parkinson’s disease in the 1990s, although the Vatican only confirmed his diagnosis in 2003.
John XXIII died in 1963 from stomach cancer that was not disclosed by the Vatican until after his death.
Benedict XVI, however, who succeeded John Paul, was the first pope to resign in 600 years, stepping down in 2013 after he said he no longer had the strength for the job.
The Vatican, long reticent to discuss papal health issues, has been unusually transparent in Leo’s case.

The pope himself announced to pilgrims in St. Peter’s Square on Sunday that a “localized nodule” had been found in his lung and he needed surgery. He also said it was detected early and was well contained.
The Vatican later provided a detailed medical bulletin hours after Leo had undergone surgery.
Another statement may be released on Wednesday afternoon, but details on the pope’s prognosis are expected to take a few days as doctors perform the necessary tests.
According to the American Cancer Society, the five-year relative survival rate for non-small cell lung cancer is 67% when the disease remains confined to the lung.
Dr. Giuseppe Cardillo, chief of thoracic surgery at Rome’s San Camillo Forlanini hospital, said removal of lung cancer discovered at an early stage usually results in an “excellent” prognosis.
Elise Allen, author of a biography of Leo for Penguin Peru, said people should not “jump the gun” in making conclusions about how the pope will recover.
“Let’s take it one day at a time,” she said. – Rappler.com

The author of The Cellist of Sarajevo alleges his career was destroyed by the allegations of rape and sexual assault, which he denies and were found unsubstantiated in a report by a former B.C. Supreme Court judge.
Galloway alleges defendants defamed him by publishing unproven allegations of sexual assault

· Posted: Oct 15, 2026 8:27 PM EDT | Last Updated: 5 minutes ago
Author and former University of British Columbia (UBC) creative writing chair Steven Galloway has concluded testifying in his defamation lawsuit trial in Vancouver.

Galloway, who alleges the defendants defamed him by publishing unproven allegations of sexual assault, took questions from Glynnis Kirchmeier, a defendant in the case who is representing herself and attending the trial remotely.

The former UBC student pressed Galloway about whether he believed she had been involved with an advocacy group for victims of sexual violence and harassment, and had also contacted other defendants, including A.B., another former student who made the allegations against Galloway.

Galloway says he found it "unlikely" Kirchmeier wasn't involved with the group because she was on one of its fundraising pages, and he recalled becoming nauseated about one of her tweets, and wondering "why is this person I’ve never met calling me a rapist?"

blocks.text: The court heard during the brief hearing in B.C. Supreme Court on Thursday that the next witness is expected to be Ronna Syed, a producer for the CBC program the fifth estate.
Galloway, who has been testifying since last week, said earlier in the trial that Syed was the first journalist to call him after the allegations surfaced, and says he told her "no comment."
Galloway filed the defamation lawsuit in 2018 but several defendants have settled with him and published public apologies.
Former UBC professor Steven Galloway’s defamation trial begins
The court heard last week that A.B.'s defence no longer includes an assertion she was assaulted by Galloway, but rather that she reported the alleged assaults.

Galloway has testified he felt ashamed at having an affair with A.B., who cannot be named due to a publication ban, but there was no prohibition on sexual relationships between faculty and students at UBC and he knew of "numerous" other examples.

articles.title: Israeli firm used ads to enable espionage, Canadian researchers say
articles.summary: An Israeli advertising agency has placed ads seen by millions of internet users that have left them open to spyware attacks, according to a new report from the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab.

image.caption: A new report by the Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto says ads placed by an Israeli firm have placed millions of internet users at risk of 'zero-click' spyware attacks. (Graeme Roy/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: World·New
An Israeli advertising agency has placed ads seen by millions of internet users that have left them open to spyware attacks, according to a new report from the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab.
Ads left millions open to 'zero-click' spyware attacks, Citizen Lab says
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 15, 2026 8:23 PM EDT | Last Updated: 37 minutes ago
The report, released on Thursday, alleges that Discover-Tech intentionally operates a platform that allows its "partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices" with spyware.
Those partners can then "push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements," it says.

Over a four-month period, Discover-Tech ads appeared on more than 120,000 websites and more than 75,000 apps in dozens of countries — endangering the security of "national-security-sensitive networks," such as government ministries, armed forces and multilateral organizations such as NATO, according to the report, which was released alongside an affiliated investigation by U.S. cybersecurity firm Confiant.

Ron Deibert, Citizen Lab's director, said the findings are a "worst-nightmare" scenario, with "two poorly regulated and highly abused industries" — targeted advertising and mercenary spyware — coming together.
"It's a recipe for disaster," Deibert told CBC News. "It's global espionage that we've uncovered on a massive scale."
'Zero-click' attacks

Rights groups have raised concerns for years about companies that sell spyware to anyone, oppressive governments in particular, wishing to spy on the public, journalists, political figures and other perceived critics.

Experts also have speculated that what's known as the targeted ad ecosystem — where data brokers and advertising firms bid in real time to place ads on apps and websites — could be used for espionage.
But Thursday's report marks the first time researchers have documented how "zero-click" spyware attacks can be enabled by targeted ads, Citizen Lab says.
"Zero-click" means that users don't need to click on a link or actively do anything for their devices to be targeted with spyware.

"The moment [the ad] is rendered, their device can be hacked, so there's really no defence against this, short of not using a smart phone or [not] connecting to the internet," Deibert said. Such infections can be hard to detect.

The report said some Discover-Tech ads also appeared on the websites of news outlets, including CBC, BBC and the New York Times. But Deibert says there's not much those organizations could have done to prevent it.
OPP may have secretly used controversial tech that can spy on citizens
"It's just the advertising ecosystem working as intended," he said.
Discover-Tech did not respond to CBC News's requests for comment via a contact form on the company's website.

Chuck Thompson, the head of public affairs at CBC, said in an email that the public broadcaster's logs have "no trace of having delivered any ads," from Discover-Tech. CBC escalated to Google, which operates systems for ad sellers, "to verify and provide answers," he said.
Al Jazeera targeted

Citizen Lab said it was able to confirm a targeted spyware attack on Al Jazeera: At least 45 of the Qatar-based news outlet's devices were infected with spyware via Discover-Tech's ads in 2024 and 2025, the report said.

When spyware is implanted, the operator behind the hack can take control of the device. "They can turn on the camera, turn on the microphone, and track someone's geolocation, so it's kind of like God-like capabilities," Deibert said.
The researchers linked the zero-click attacks on Al Jazeera "with high confidence" to spyware from Candiru, an Israel-based firm that the report said has rebranded as Integrity Labs.
LISTEN | How spyware abusers can easily hack your phone:
Ideas53:59Spyware abusers can easily hack your phone and surveil you

In 2021, the U.S. Department of Commerce sanctioned Candiru "based on evidence that [it] developed and supplied spyware to foreign governments that used these tools to maliciously target government officials, journalists, businesspeople, activists, academics, and embassy workers."
CBC News could not immediately find a way to reach Candiru on Thursday. The Reuters news agency also said its attempts were not successful.
An Al Jazeera spokesperson condemned the targeting of its staff by such spyware as 'deliberate attack on journalists and on press freedom.' (Malak Harb/The Associated Press)
An Al Jazeera Media Network spokesperson told CBC News in an email that it "strongly condemns the targeting of our staff with mercenary spyware."

"This is a deliberate attack on journalists and on press freedom," the spokesperson said, adding that while Al Jazeera would not speculate on who deployed the spyware, it is calling for "a full, independent investigation to identify those responsible and hold them to account."
Push for investigations

Qing Tan, an associate professor at Athabasca University in Alberta, said the Citizen Lab report raises "very concerning" questions, including around personal privacy. "A majority of people don't realize this could happen to them, so this is a very big issue," he said.
Citizen Lab researchers said their findings should push ad vendors to "significantly level up their cybersecurity and threat detection capacity to effectively cut off malicious advertisers."
They also called on regulators around the world to "investigate whether the rights of their citizens, as well as applicable privacy and security laws were violated."

items: To censor the internet, 10 countries use Canadian filtering technology, researchers say
Ontario police may have secretly used controversial Israeli spyware, report finds
Your phone could easily be tapped by spyware abusers: cybersecurity expert

blocks.text: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada did not immediately respond to emailed questions about whether it intends to investigate the report's allegations or take any immediate action.

A Google spokesperson told CBC News in an emailed statement that it blocked Discover-Tech from its ad platforms "for systematically violating" the company's policies, and that it has set up warnings "to help protect people if they navigate to websites linked to this group," they said.

IAB Europe, a European association that develops frameworks for digital marketing and the advertising ecosystem, also said Thursday that Discover-Tech was suspended from its list of global vendors for violating its terms.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jillian Kestler-D'Amours is a senior writer at CBC based in Montreal. You can reach her at jillian.kestler-d.amours@cbc.ca.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Marcos statement claiming to cancel 2028 election is taken out of context
articles.summary: He was actually addressing Vice President Sara Duterte’s claims that he is pushing for charter change to cancel elections

blocks.text: Claim: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. slipped up and revealed that he plans to amend the Constitution to prevent national elections from being held in 2028.

Why we fact-checked this: Multiple videos circulating online showed Marcos in an interview with the media, supposedly berating Palace Press Officer Castro for revealing his reaction to the plans to change the Constitution.
“Bakit mo sinabi sa kanila ‘yan? That was only supposed to be the two of us. That was – my reaction was to changing the Constitution to, ano, the elections,” Marcos said in the video.
(Why did you tell them that? That was only supposed to be the two of us. That was – my reaction was to changing the Constitution to, what, the elections.)

Facebook user Vlog Ranz overlaid text on the video that says, “Huli sa bibig; no elections sa 2028.” (Caught by one’s own words; no elections in 2028.)Dan-agan Balita, another Facebook user, did the same and wrote: “Binuking ang sarili dahil kay payaso Castro. Huli tuloy sa planong no elections.” (He exposed himself because of that clown Castro. Now, the “no-election” plan has been exposed.)
Combined, the two posts have 3,900 reactions, 933 comments, and 1,590 shares as of writing. Multiple users also reposted the video bearing the same claim about the elections.

The facts: There is no official announcement that there would be no elections in 2028. Though genuine, the video takes Marcos out of context; he was actually addressing Castro’s response to the media, in relation to his supposed reaction toward Vice President Sara Duterte’s claims that he was pushing for charter change to cancel elections.

On September 26, Duterte denied knowing and having involvement with Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., a former member of the Philippine National Police (PNP), who claimed he had delivered millions of pesos to her. She argued that it was another media stunt orchestrated by the government.
She wrote in a statement: “The desperation of the administration to bring me down, push for Charter Change, prevent the 2028 elections, and cling to power is becoming increasingly diabolical.”

In a September 28 press briefing, Castro delivered Marcos’ supposed reaction to this and said, “Ang sabi po niya, ‘yan po ay nonsense, fake news, mahilig magsinungaling – mga buwaon (liar).” (He said that it is nonsense, fake news, that they are fond of lying; they are liars.)
Eventually, at the Kapihan with The Media in Singapore on October 11, Marcos responded to a reporter who asked for a follow-up on Castro’s statement.

Based on the Presidential Communications Office’s official transcript, he said, “Claire, ba’t mo sinabi sa kanila ‘yan? That was only supposed to be…[inaudible] That was my reaction was to changing the Constitution to the elections. Kasama ‘yun eh, sa quotation na ‘yun. Iyan ang reaction ko.”

(Claire, why did you tell them that? That was only supposed to be… [inaudible] That was my reaction regarding the shift from amending the Constitution to the elections. That was part of it—part of that quote. That was my reaction.)

Charter change: The President expressed openness to changing the 1987 Constitution’s economic provisions to attract foreign investors, but did not say anything about preventing any election from happening.
Duterte insisted multiple times in her statements that Marcos has allegedly been pushing for a charter change to extend his term and stay in power. The latter has continuously denied the claims.
Other fact-checks: Rappler has previously debunked numerous false claims surrounding Marcos:

items: FACT CHECK: Marcos did not say he wants another 6-year presidential term
FACT CHECK: Marcos Jr. did not say protecting VP Duterte from her case is ‘corruption’
FACT CHECK: Video of Claire Castro calling Marcos a ‘drug addict’ is altered
FACT CHECK: Contrary to claim, Marcos has no plans to resign
FACT CHECK: Congress did not vote on any new impeachment case vs Marcos

blocks.text: – Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: [Market Rider] Buy when there’s blood in the streets, even if it’s your own blood.
articles.summary: The best time to buy assets or invest money is during a severe market crash or panic, when everyone else is terrified and selling

blocks.text: The best time to buy assets or invest money is during a severe market crash or panic, when everyone else is terrified and selling

items: Estella Dhiel B. Villamiel presented a sobering economic overview of the Philippines, highlighting severe external headwinds, including rising oil prices and inflation, which have led to a slowdown in GDP growth and increased financial distress among households.

The Philippine economy's GDP growth has slowed to 2.6%, with household consumption and capital formation declining significantly, while inflation reached 7.2%, prompting the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas to raise interest rates to combat rising prices.

Villamiel suggested that economic recovery is contingent on resolving the Middle East shipping bottleneck, which could stabilize oil prices and ease inflation, although the likelihood of a quick resolution to the US-Iran conflict remains low.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Last Monday, October 12, a discussion on the current state of the economy was held by the members of the Monday Circle. The talk was led by Estella Dhiel B. Villamiel, who serves as the head of institutional research at First Metro Securities Brokerage Corporation (FirstMetroSec) and is an active member of the select group. The update revealed sobering realities about the economy especially for its near-term status that would explain the reasons behind the present variable softness of the stock market – bringing to mind the trading strategy of the market adage, “Buy when there’s blood in the streets, even if it’s your own blood.”

blocks.caption: AT A GLANCE. Estella Dhiel Villamiel, head of institutional research at First Metro Securities Brokerage Corporation, gives a presentation on the Philippine economy to the Monday Circle on October 12, 2026 at the Westin Manila hotel in Mandaluyong City.

blocks.text: The axiom is also sometimes paraphrased into “in your hand.” Nevertheless, it is a foundational maxim of contrarian investing. It means that the absolute best time to buy assets or invest money is during a severe market crash or panic, when everyone else is terrified and selling.

While the imagery projected by the adage refers to a market in total chaos, we are not yet there, according to the presentation of Villamiel. So far, the problem is about structural headwinds rather than about catastrophic panic. But, come to think of it, we could just be a blink away from it considering what is happening in and out of the country.

Titled “The Philippine Economy At A Glance,” Villamiel described the macroeconomic overview of the Philippine economy to be under severe external headwinds, primarily driven by the economic strain caused by an external oil shock triggered by a US-Iran war, which has created a negative domestic transmission chain, namely: rising oil prices, a widening import bill, a weakening Philippine peso, and elevated inflation.

The country’s gross domestic product (GDP) from January to June this year has slowed down to 2.6%. Outside of the pandemic years, this represents the slowest economic expansion the country has experienced in nearly two decades since 2009. To achieve the government’s full-year target of 3.5% to 4.5%, the economy must expand at a much faster rate of 4.4% to 6.4% in the second half (2Q) of the year.

Looking at the demand-side breakdown, household consumption growth has cooled down from historical highs down to 1.9% in 2Q26. This means consumers are in “survival mode.” This is worrying because the people are sticking to buying essential goods for they are paying at higher prices for lesser quantities.
Capital formation (investments) has, as well, sharply fallen, dropping by -9.2% year-on-year (YoY) in 2Q of 2026, severely weighing on economic momentum.

Complicating the situation, inflation hit 7.2% in September, bringing the year-to-date (YTD) average at 5.4%. This is way past the 2% to 4% comfort band of the government. Driving the economy in this situation are transport and food costs due to high fuel prices, with local transport sharing a 65% correlation with Brent crude prices. Full-year inflation is projected at 6.1%.

To stop prices from rising even more and to protect the peso, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) raised its target reverse repurchase (RRP) rate to 5.0% last August 27. This measure made loans, mortgages, and credit card debt much costlier than before. Due to this rate increase, car sales growth – excluding electric vehicles – has plummeted sharply into negative territory, hitting roughly -10% YoY by the end of August 2026. People are just pulling back on big-ticket items like cars because loans are too expensive.
On the fiscal side, the first half 2026 budget deficit reached 5.8% of GDP, pushing the national debt-to-GDP ratio to an elevated 66%.

Credit card usage also reached historic highs. Unfortunately, this shift has triggered a 46.4% spike in non-performing credit card debt, signaling that a growing number of households are facing severe financial distress.

Because the Philippines is a net importer of fuel, higher energy costs require a larger outflow of US dollars to sustain domestic consumption. With such, the peso has experienced significant depreciation against the US dollar, primarily driven by escalating global oil prices.

Concurrently, the domestic job market exhibits underlying structural weaknesses despite stable headline employment figures claiming 94% to 96% full employment. The rolling 12-month net job metrics register a structural loss of 307,000 jobs, signaling contraction in key employment sectors as unemployment rose to 5.3%, up from 3.9% last year.

Furthermore, rising underemployment rates as manifested through the number of workers seeking additional hours, indicating that existing positions fail to provide sufficient income to meet the cost of living.
Instead of concluding her assessment on how much more the economy may suffer, Villamiel ended her presentation on what could trigger the recovery of the economy.
According to her, economic recovery for the country is fundamentally conditional on resolving the Middle East shipping bottleneck.

If commercial vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz recovers from current single-digit daily lows back to its pre-war average of about 33 per day, the following stabilization sequence will occur: global oil risk premiums will drop, directly cooling domestic transport CPI; the import bill will narrow, relieving pressure on Gross International Reserves (estimated at US$100 billion) and allowing the peso to strengthen; and easing inflation will allow the BSP to halt or reverse rate hikes, reviving depressed household credit and corporate capital expenditure.

I agree with Villamiel’s position that the current market fall and the economy’s problem of being squeezed by high prices, weak growth, skyrocketing energy costs, a widening import bill, a depreciating Philippine peso, and elevated inflation, could possibly bottom out and come to an end in a short time with the Middle East shipping bottleneck being resolved soon.
On the other hand, the chances of the US-Iran war ending soon is said to be low, as diplomatic talks have stalled and military escalations have intensified in recent days.

But like the way how the contrarian strategy works, it may be hard to imagine under the present circumstances, the shipping bottleneck in the Middle East could just be resolved sooner than is expected. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses
articles.summary:
Moscow sends swarms of drones to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine as Zelenskyy says Kyiv will restart strikes on Russian oil refineries

The White House’s unilateral effort to…

blocks.text: The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries despite warnings from Donald Trump.

Moscow accused Ukraine of launching a strike against a Russian oil refinery in the Ryazan region, its first since Trump abruptly declared an “energy ceasefire” that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to.
Trump has demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy stop attacking Russian oil refineries, claiming it is the cause of a global rise in the price of diesel fuel.
An attack on two neutral ships in Romanian territorial waters at the mouth of the Danube River indicated that strikes against vulnerable commercial targets are set to expand.

The Romanian president, Nicușor Dan, said two Russian drones violated Romanian airspace and struck two chemical tankers, setting the ships ablaze. Rescue crews were searching for at least seven missing sailors.

“The situation in the Black Sea is serious,” he said. “Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk. Seafarers killed, injured and missing, very close to the shores of Romania and Bulgaria. This is unacceptable and it has to stop.”

blocks.caption: A San Marino-flagged ship caught fire in Romanian territorial waters. Photograph: Romanian interior ministry/Reuters

blocks.text: Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, after briefly halting them to demonstrate that Ukraine was ready for peace talks. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told the Financial Times. He also attacked a gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”.

Images from Ryazan showed flames at the refinery, which regional officials said had been targeted by 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. Moscow claimed debris from a drone struck by anti-aircraft fire had hit the refinery and sparked the fire.

Ukraine also struck back at Russia’s military, hitting four Sukhoi Su-34 fighter/bomber jets and damaging two more, according to Zelenskyy. Ukraine’s military said it had used a Neptune cruise missile to strike an airfield in Russia’s southern Voronezh region.
“These very warplanes were ready to launch new attacks on Ukraine and were loaded with aerial bombs,” Zelenskyy said, publishing a satellite photo of the damaged airfield.

blocks.caption: Destruction at Borisoglebsk airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region. Photograph: Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS/Reuters

blocks.text: In Ukraine, more than 360 Russian drones targeted Kirovohrad, a central region that has been hit less hard than others closer to Russia, in attacks that killed three people and injured six.
“The enemy deliberately hit critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics ⁠facilities and residential homes,” the regional governor, Andriy Raikovych, said in a statement.

Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 850 Shahed drones at a time when the speed of Ukraine’s defensive capabilities was being “artificially restricted”, a reference to sudden limitations on Ukraine’s use of the Starlink and Starshield mobile internet terminals.

“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in a social media post on X, referring to a growing quarrel with the Trump administration.

“Ukraine needs steady support, above all in defending our skies. We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security,” he said.

Later, the British defence secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC that he had been “reassured directly” by his US counterpart Pete Hegseth that access to the vital Starlink communications system had been restored. The defence secretary said it was not yet clear to the UK why the disruption occurred, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.”

blocks.caption: Wreckage of a Russian jet-powered drone lies inside a crater that appeared at the site of a residential area after a strike in Kyiv. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters

blocks.text: Trump suddenly declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, writing on TruthSocial: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!”

Despite Trump’s claims, however, Russia continued to launch heavy strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, using hypersonic and ballistic missiles to target key Ukrainian power plants, leaving cities including Kyiv without power and water for hours. Ukraine said it would not strike Russian oil refineries in the interim in order to show that it was ready for negotiations.
But the White House piled pressure on Zelenskyy to capitulate to Russia by threatening to cut programmes to deliver arms to Ukraine and to stop sharing US battlefield intelligence with Ukraine.

The US appeared to make good on some threats. Ukraine said it had not received advance warning from Washington of Russian missile strikes for several days this week. And on Wednesday, Ukrainian soldiers complained that their access to Starshield programmes controlled by the US military had been restricted, scuppering drone missions on the frontlines.

On Thursday, a group of US senators from both major parties sent a letter to the Pentagon demanding it investigate whether the satellite and intelligence services had been deliberately restricted, and whether the Trump administration was responsible.

“We are particularly alarmed by incidents in which U.S. diplomatic, military and security personnel were unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids, amid reported disruptions to intelligence-sharing and early-warning capabilities,” they wrote, according to the New York Times.

The feud between Zelenskyy and Trump has spun out of control over the last week. Trump, who believes his support for Ukraine should come with a degree of control over the country’s leadership, has said Ukraine should “get a new president”.
Zelenskyy, when asked on Thursday by Piers Morgan whether he felt betrayed, said yes. “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner,” he said.
Musk, the head of SpaceX, which produces the Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military, has emerged as a leading critic of Zelenskyy in the US.

On Thursday, Musk denied throttling the Starlink systems and said they were controlled by the US government. But in a social media post commenting on a Zelenskyy statement that Ukraine would continue to fight until Russia’s defeat, he wrote: “And so the slaughter continues … Time for Zelensky to go.”

articles.title: DFA admonishes China envoy over ‘thinly veiled threat on use of force’
articles.summary: Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan asserts that Beijing is no troublemaker while saying Manila should 'feel fortunate' that China does not use force, even though it could 'easily win' if it does

blocks.text: PH-CHINA TIES. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. summons Chinese ambassador Jing Quan over maritime incident at the Ayungin Shoal in July 2026.
Malacañang
Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan asserts that Beijing is no troublemaker while saying Manila should 'feel fortunate' that China does not use force, even though it could 'easily win' if it does

items: The Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs criticized Chinese diplomat Jing Quan for making remarks that implied a threat of force, emphasizing the need for diplomatic tact.

Jing's comments come amid ongoing tensions between the Philippines and China, particularly regarding the South China Sea, with the Philippines rejecting claims that military communication issues are to blame for the tensions.

The relationship between the two countries has been complicated by China's aggressive maritime actions and its refusal to acknowledge the Philippines' rights in the West Philippine Sea, despite hopes for a diplomatic reset under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), in a rare public admonishment late Thursday, October 15, said it was “regrettable” that Beijing’s top diplomat to Manila, Jing Quan, “had a poor choice of words that would seem to convey a thinly veiled threat of the use of force.”

In a chance interview with reporters earlier on Thursday, Jing denied that China was a troublemaker in the region and blamed the Philippines — or at least Philippine officials — for causing tensions between the two Asian countries.

Talking to Philippine reporters, he added: “We should feel fortunate enough that you have a neighbor like China in this region. If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we’ll not use force. We love peace.”
Jing is a veteran diplomat who spent years in the United States before being assigned to the Philippines in late 2025.

blocks.caption: Hindi Ito Marites: Easing tensions between the Philippines and China

blocks.text: “The business of diplomacy requires tact and restraint in order to create space necessary for discourse, dialogue and engagement, regardless of the disparity in positions or perspectives,” said the DFA in a statement reacting to Jing’s remarks, which it said were “hardly helpful in the context of the complicated bilateral ties between the Philippines and China.”

“It is hoped that all diplomats accredited to the Philippines take greater care in the language used in public statements so as not to further erode mutual trust and confidence, nor derail the advancement of dialogue and constructive engagement,” added the DFA in a statement released through its West Philippine Sea spokesperson Rogelio Villanueva Jr..

The latest chapter in the long-running war of words between the Philippines and China has seen the Chinese embassy in Manila making posts to blame Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.’s policy of cutting off military-to-military communication for escalating tensions at sea.

The Philippine military has rejected the claim, telling reporters that the absence of direct communication channels with China’s military is not to blame for the tensions, which it has attributed to aggressive actions by Chinese maritime forces. That the Philippine military is not allowed to directly engage with the People’s Liberation Army is not exactly new information, either. Teodoro has made no secret of this decision for years.

Jing’s remarks would not be the first time a Chinese diplomat has made veiled threats — threadbare as they may be — against the Philippines. His immediate predecessor, Huang Xilian, was also criticized in April 2023 for warning against closer military and defense ties with the Philippine’s treaty-ally the United States, or siding with Taiwan independence, lest the safety of overseas Filipino workers in the independently-governed island be compromised.

The Chinese embassy’s messaging and public communications strategies have changed dramatically since Jing took over in late 2025. Beijing’s embassy in Manila has been combative toward Filipino officials — mostly spokespersons from defense and security agencies and, occasionally, even nationally elected officials — in its public statements.
Jing’s latest remarks comes 10 months into what President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and the DFA have hoped to be a year of “reset” in bilateral ties between Manila and Beijing.
The two Asian neighbors have close trade ties but diverge dramatically when it comes to talk of the South China Sea — in particular, the area called the West Philippine Sea.

Beijing claims almost all of the vast waterway, including areas that are part of the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone. China refuses to acknowledge the landmark 2016 Arbitral Award, which affirmed the Philippines’ EEZ and found China’s supposed historical claim invalid.

Under Marcos, Manila has been both assertive and transparent in protecting both its sovereignty claims and rights in the West Philippine Sea. China’s claims have meant that, for Filipino frontliners — the Navy, Coast Guard and even fisherfolk — harassment at the hands of Chinese maritime agencies is a risk in flashpoints in those waters. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Tip-off foiled US teen suspect's plot to attack Hindu temple, police say
articles.summary: The alleged plot only failed because the 19-year-old suspect's gun jammed outside the place of worship, say police.

blocks.text: A Taco Bell cashier's alleged plot for a mass shooting at a Hindu temple near Chicago was thwarted by a tip-off from one of his colleagues, investigators say.
Alexandros Paporakis, 19, from Palatine, Illinois, appeared in court on Wednesday charged with one count of making a terrorist threat and one count of unlawful possession of a weapon.
Paporakis allegedly sent a message about the planned attack on Sunday to the co-worker, who alerted authorities, officials said.
Police said they found writings in which Paporakis identified as a white supremacist and wrote about his hatred for non-white people.
Palatine police chief William Nord said on Thursday they were notified about a mass shooting plot on Sunday by someone who had received "concerning electronic communications" from Paporakis.
"These communications played a vital role in bringing this matter to the attention of law enforcement," said the police chief.
According to CBS, the BBC's US partner, prosecutors said the tipster had worked with Paporakis.
Nord said a red Honda RDX registered to Paporakis entered the car park of a "known Hindu temple" in the suburb of Aurora at Sunday lunchtime.
The suspect allegedly tried to open fire, but the gun jammed, so he drove home, where he lived with his mother.
According to NBC Chicago, Paporakis told his colleague over phone messages that his gun had jammed and he got out of there "super-fast".
Once home, he "searched internet trying to learn how to unjam his gun & called a colleague informing them of [his] intent to carry out a mass shooting", reports NBC Chicago.
He is thought to have acted alone.
The police chief said officers had searched Paporakis' home, where they found a rifle, loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds of rifle ammunition and body armour.
Nord said they also discovered an eight-page document by the suspect containing "extremist ideologies" and revealing his plans for an attack.
In the writings, he described himself as a "sociopathic white supremacist neo-Nazi", according to CBS.
Police have questioned Paporakis' mother, who was said to be unco-operative.
The Hindu temple identified by local media as the intended target said it had implemented new security measures.
India's Ministry of External Affairs said the incident "adds to growing concerns over racist hostility and anti-India hate in the US".
US congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois said he was "horrified" by the incident.
In a Facebook statement, he said he and his family worship at the temple and were there last Sunday.
The Chicago metropolitan area is home to one of the biggest Indian-American populations in the US.

articles.title: Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
articles.summary: France's prime minister has suggested that student anger is being weaponised, as the unions and other protesters prepare to take to the streets too.

blocks.text: The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe.

Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs.
For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets.
This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France.
Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement.
France's prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election.
The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.
Jérôme Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations.
The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video.
"Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added.
So what is going on in the EU's second largest economy?

Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt.
Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of?
"You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me.
She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt.

"The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary."

"Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates.
"The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself."
"Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes.
Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected.
But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further.
France's national motto is liberté, égalité, fraternité (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts.
I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest.

They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs.
"France likes to speak of égalité," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit."
None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway.
The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities.
They are part of a defiant French tradition.

Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les Misérables, also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: "Si vous n'êtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas."
("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.")
Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity."
Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response.
Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in.

This came after mounting accusations of police brutality, denied by France's interior ministry, during protests earlier this month in which hundreds were injured and a 15-year-old boy in the town of Lens lost a hand.
France's interior minister has since suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations.

Gwen told me she did not mind that her son was missing weeks of school as a result of the lock-ins. "It's a far better education for him to wake up to his civic duty and to fight for what is just in society," she said.
At Thursday's demo I also came across 17-year-old Lola and her mother, Sandrine, sharing a placard that said revolution was the most beautiful expression of humanity.
"My mum took to the streets in '68," Lola said proudly. "Now it's my turn. No point in waiting for the presidential election in France. We want change now."

Student protests in Paris in May 1968 are the stuff of legend in France. Demands for better education inspired workers to join the marches which turned into the ­biggest general strike in French ­history. It set the standard for revolutionary upheaval for a generation and is credited with creating new opportunities for the French left.

Now, though, with six months to go before an already fraught presidential election in France, there are accusations that the hard left, under presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is weaponising student frustration.

"Members of [Mélenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage," said Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday. He accused them of encouraging protests, then going through the motions of condemning any violence.
"This hypocrisy damages France," said Lecornu.
But "Mélenchon for President!" is a chant you often hear amongst the students in the streets.

Supporters applaud his desire for a wealth tax in France, for lowering the voting age to 16 and for being the only presidential candidate to turn up to French schools to examine the state of them, several demonstrators told me.
For Marine Le Pen, the nationalist anti-immigration favourite in France's presidential race, the solution is cutting the country's €11bn contribution to the EU's budget.
There is, though, reason to doubt that any new French president, from the left or the right, will be able to break the impasse over France's finances.

France is far from alone in Europe right now faced with an ageing population, a generous welfare state to run and a national economy squeezed by outside pressures such as US President Donald Trump's trade tariffs and the war in the Persian Gulf.

Whether in France, Germany, Sweden or Italy, there is an inherent tension between politicians who hesitate to tell voters the truth about shrinking public finances, the defence establishment's demand for higher defence spending and citizens' insistence on improved public services.
In France, that pressure is particularly acute. French public expenditure, at about 57% GDP, is one of the steepest amongst wealthy nations worldwide.

Social spending, particularly on pensions, is exceptionally large, while French citizens pay one of the highest overall tax and social contribution burdens in Europe. Simply put, they expect a welfare and public service bang for their buck.
But economist Anne-Laure Delatte does not believe having a new president will ease her country's financial migraine.
"We need constitutional change. A new system. A new Republic," she told me.
"Our Fifth Republic is centred around a powerful president. Parliament is there to block him or her rather than to find consensus or to make new laws."
For France to progress, she says, that has to change.

The French parliamentary election that follows the 2027 presidential vote is likely to be as divided as ever, she believes: "We need a system where MPs have more power and should learn consensus and coalition-building from our European neighbours."
In her opinion, education had to be protected and funds better distributed. It was an investment in France's financial future, she told me.

"Our current system of inequality in schooling and low wages for teachers means we lose out from benefiting from the best and brightest across French society. That is not only unfair on individuals but our economy ultimately loses out on innovation and productivity."
Re-writing France's constitution is not on the cards, at the moment. So, what about the here and now, I asked centrist politician Anne-Catherine Loisier.
She's a senator for the Centrist Union in France's upper house of parliament and vice president of the parliamentary group for sciences and technology.
Loisier, along with pretty much every leading French politician across the political spectrum, says the protesting students "must feel heard".

"Our budgets are limited," she admitted, "but you don't necessarily need more money. You can make improvements by redistributing funding better. Education is a regional competence in France. Every region should take a look at local needs and address priorities accordingly. That action can be taken immediately."

I asked Loisier if she agreed with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, that regions should be given greater powers. "Absolutely," she replied. "France has traditionally been very Paris-centric but so much could be improved by decentralising the country."

"My France isn't broken. I don't recognise that image you see portrayed in the media. My country is made up of lots of Frances. Paris, the regions; northern and southern France. We need to give power back to the people. Local governments can look people in the eye directly, so voters feel they have power over their own future, rather than politicians handing them their fate from up high in Paris."
"That way I hope we can restore voters' - and students' - faith in politics."
It's a promise you hear from politicians - right and left - ahead of France's huge elections next year.
But opinion polls here, as across most of Europe, indicate public faith in the political class is in dwindling supply.

articles.title: Lawyer urges Supreme Court to clarify ruling on senior discounts, promos
articles.summary: In a statement on Thursday, October 15, senior citizen advocate lawyer Romulo Macalintal warned that the decision could be exploited by business establishments to evade granting

blocks.text: October 16, 2026 | 7:00am
The logo of the Supreme Court at the Supreme Court Building in Manila.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court should issue a clear elaboration on its ruling barring the application of a senior citizen discount after other promotional discounts have been applied, a senior citizen advocate said.

In a statement on Thursday, October 15, senior citizen advocate and lawyer Romulo Macalintal warned that the decision could be exploited by business establishments to evade granting senior citizen discounts.

According to the Supreme Court’s ruling released in a press briefer on October 14, senior citizens cannot stack their statutory 20% discount on top of existing promotional prices, reinforcing that elderly consumers must choose between the promotional price and the statutory 20% discount, whichever yields greater savings.

While the ruling acquitted a hotel executive in Bacolod City after finding that the guests had already received a 20% discount through a pre-negotiated group rate, Macalintal emphasized that the public briefer lacks critical legal distinctions.
Macalintal pointed out that the denial of the discount in the Bacolod hotel case stemmed specifically from a pre-negotiated group association rate rather than a standard commercial sales promotion.

Without explicit clarification from the justices, he warned that commercial establishments might improperly label regular transactions or self-run "house promos" as promotional offers to deny elderly customers their rightful 20% discount.

“This clarification is very crucial and imperative because establishments may have the impression that they can just conduct promos on their own or run house promos to deny a senior citizen their 20% discount,” Macalintal’s statement read.

“This distinction is vital. Without it, establishments might falsely label regular transactions as ‘promos’ to evade granting senior discounts, entirely defeating the protective intent of the law,” he added.

Addressing the legal mechanism behind promotional pricing, Macalintal stressed that under Article 116 of Republic Act No. 7394, or the Consumer Act of the Philippines, any company intending to conduct a promotional campaign must first secure a permit from the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) before launching the offer.

According to Macalintal, an establishment cannot legally invoke the non-concurrence or "double-discount" rule unless the promotion has prior approval from the DTI and is set for a specified timeframe.
“Clearly, an establishment conducting a promo without a DTI permit is still obligated to extend to a senior citizen the 20% discount over and above the unauthorized promo price,” Macalintal said.
Macalintal also pointed out that the prohibition against double-discounting does not strip senior citizens of their statutory value-added tax exemption.

He also urged the high court to clarify in its full written decision that senior citizens utilizing hotel services remain entitled to their 12% VAT exemption alongside their applicable price reduction.

articles.title: How did a P.E.I. cold case fall apart just before it was set to go to trial?
articles.summary: There are still unanswered questions about how Charlottetown Police Services handled a high-profile P.E.I. cold case after all charges against the accused were dropped just before the case was set to…

blocks.text: Criminologist weighs in on Charlottetown police's handling of Byron Carr murder investigation

There are still unanswered questions about how Charlottetown Police Services handled a high-profile P.E.I. cold case after all charges against the accused were dropped just before the case was set to go to trial.

The provincial Crown Attorney’s Office announced Tuesday that the charges against Todd Joseph Irving in connection with the 1988 killing of P.E.I. teacher Byron Carr were being withdrawn after it came to light that Charlottetown police had lost "extensive crucial evidence" in the case.

CBC News first learned about that missing evidence — which includes the knife found at the scene and the towel used to strangle Carr — at a bail hearing in July. The Crown confirmed that’s when they first learned about it, too. But Charlottetown police later told CBC News they knew physical evidence was missing as far back as 2007 when the case was reopened.

items: Charges were dropped in a decades-old murder case. Now, there are calls for an independent review
Charlottetown police lost the evidence in a P.E.I. cold-case murder. How did it happen?

blocks.text: Interim Charlottetown police Chief Darren MacDougall believes police did tell the Crown at some point that some items were missing, but not the full picture of how much physical evidence or exactly which items were lost.
He acknowledges that information should have been provided to the Crown sooner.

"There was likely not enough transparency with regard to the evidence as it relates to the Crown and the investigators. So there was certainly a breakdown there. I think that the investigators clung to the hope that they would be able to interview some of the people involved in 1989 to determine where they might have put these exhibits," MacDougall said.
"It’s the responsibility of the police, for full disclosure, to move that disclosure to the Crown."

But MacDougall was quick to point out that the DNA evidence collected from the items wasn’t lost — that material was processed and stored appropriately. It was the items themselves, after they’d been processed and sent back to Charlottetown police, that were misplaced.
Calls mount for an investigation into how crucial evidence in P.E.I. murder case was lost
Michael Arntfield is a professor and criminologist at Western University who heads up the school’s cold case research group. He’s also a former police detective.

"It’s both unusual and unfortunate because this was a great solve using state-of-the art investigative genetic genealogy, IGG, to track down the still alleged or once alleged offender in a very infamous cold case," he said.

"However, it turned out to be sort of an exploding cigar in that once, sort of, the novelty of the solve subsided … the two key pieces of evidence seem to have disappeared, which sort of pulls the rug out from underneath the whole case."
'It contaminates the whole investigation'
Arntfield believes police were hoping the DNA evidence was incontrovertible. And police have said as much.
Todd Joseph Irving walked out of court on Tuesday a free man after the charges against him in connection with the death of Byron Carr were dropped. (CBC)

"With the evidence that we relied upon, and we had significant forensic DNA evidence, we believed the evidence met the threshold to believe that [Irving] committed the offense," MacDougall said in an interview with CBC News after the charges were dropped.
At the July bail hearing, police testified that Irving's DNA was found on Carr’s body, on a pair of underwear left at the scene and on an extinguished cigarette butt placed in Carr’s navel.

His DNA was not found on the towel used to strangle Carr or on a sock left at the crime scene that police said was likely used as a glove to prevent leaving fingerprints behind, according to police testimony.

The entirety of the missing evidence isn’t clear, but the Crown described it as "the overwhelming majority of the critical physical evidence," going on to say that included "key exhibits central to the prosecution."

items: Family of Byron Carr speaks out after murder charges in decades-old cold case withdrawn
Charges laid in decades-old P.E.I. cold case murder withdrawn after key evidence lost

blocks.text: With that, Arntfield said, the credibility of the Charlottetown Police Services is lost — along with whatever remaining evidence they had.

"It contaminates the whole investigation because a judge or jury or both … would be left wondering, 'OK, if they have slipshod record-keeping and no chain of custody for key exhibits, what else don’t we know? What else was overlooked? What other corners were cut?'" he said.

"This isn’t corruption, this isn’t malicious. What I think it is is they were fixated on solving this, they cut corners and ultimately at the end of the day they were motivated by getting an alleged killer off the streets and ensuring justice for the family decades later."
What happened to missing evidence in the Byron Carr murder case? Charlottetown's interim police chief explains
If police had been forthcoming with the Crown about what physical evidence they did — and didn’t — have in their possession, Arntfield said the outcome could have been much different.

"You would think in a case like this — a high-profile historical homicide using a state-of-the-art and still somewhat controversial technology, IGG — that, even just as a courtesy, some senior officer or the case manager might have notified the Crown that a complex, high-profile case is coming down the pipe, apprise them of the strengths and weaknesses of the case, what witnesses are still alive and locatable and exhibits are still intact," he said.

"There’s other things that could have been done based on what police knew in order to shore up those deficiencies.… I think they would have had probably more evidence to incentivize maybe a quick guilty plea, which is I’m almost certain what police were relying on here. They were expecting a quick guilty plea and none of this suspicious disappearance of evidence would have ever seen the light of day."
Police, Crown look through different lenses: MacDougall
In Ontario, Arntfield said, cold cases get what he calls a "concierge approach," where the Crown is brought in early to weigh in on the strength of the evidence.
MacDougall acknowledges that, in this case, investigators were perhaps weighing the strength of the evidence differently than a prosecutor might.

"Perhaps the Crown, who views this through a different lens — the weight that existed with the missing exhibits measured with the weight of the DNA evidence, the forensic DNA evidence that was very compelling, I would say — [the Crown], again viewing it through a different lens, they came to the conclusion that they were unable to provide the accused with a fair trial."
Darren MacDougall, Charlottetown's interim police chief, says he would welcome an independent investigation. (Barry Acton/CBC)
While Arntfield called the outcome of this case a rare and regrettable snafu, he said it shouldn’t erode public confidence in police.

"The investigation was solid, there was a chokepoint along the way where something happened and I wouldn’t even call it a coverup, I would say they strategically omitted that information at the last minute," he said.
"The question will be: who made the determination to suppress this glaring deficiency and suspicious disappearance and proceed at great time and expense?"
There have been calls for an independent review of how the case was handled, which MacDougall said he would welcome.

It’s up to P.E.I.'s justice and public safety minister to call such an investigation. In a statement to CBC News, the department said it was communicating with Charlottetown police about the Byron Carr case, saying "government has various options to consider in terms of a review and scope, so a particular path is not set yet. It's still under discussion."
Why were all charges dropped in the P.E.I. cold-case murder of Byron Carr?

articles.title: Oregon school shooting: Gunman kills 3 students and teacher before being shot dead by community member
articles.summary: A 16-year-old gunman opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, killing three children and a teacher. Two others were wounded. A community member pursued and killed the suspected shooter,…

image.caption: A shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, has left multiple victims, police said Thursday.Image: Joe Kline/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A 16-year-old gunman killed three children and a teacher and wounded two others in a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday before a community member pursued and killed him, authorities said.
"The deceased at the scene include three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and one teacher," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told reporters. Another child and a teacher were injured and taken to a hospital.
The first 911 call came in around 1 p.m. local time (2000 GMT) from a person in a vehicle outside Silver Rail Elementary who reported being shot at by someone carrying a long gun, Krantz said.
Additional 911 calls came from inside the school, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said. Officers arrived within minutes.
"Seconds later, we received word over the radio that the suspect in this incident was down," Miller said.
Students evacuated as police respond to shooting
Bend is a ​city of some ‌100,000 people in central Oregon, about 175 miles (280 kilometers) southeast of Portland.

blocks.caption: Students were evacuated from the school and the buildings were cordoned offImage: Joe Kline/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: An updated post later said law enforcement was escorting students by bus to a separate location, where they could reunite with their families. The school serves kindergarten through fifth grade, roughly children aged ⁠5 to ​11. It has about 450 students and 40 staff members, Miller said.
Oregon Governor Tina Kotek thanked the community member who "heroically intervened to ​stop further loss of life."

"No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have ​to live through ‌this kind of day. And as we learn more about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured, and their families and their loved ones, we are going to do a lot of crying, and we are going to cry together, and we're probably going to ‌cry privately," Kotek said.
US grapples with recurring mass shootings

The United States, where firearms are widely available, experiences frequent gun violence, with thousands of people killed each year. It has the highest rate of gun-related deaths among high-income countries.

blocks.caption: Emergency personnel directed people away from the schoolImage: Rob Kerr/REUTERS

blocks.text: The deadliest school shooting in US history took place at Virginia Tech on April 16, 2007. South Korean student Seung-Hui Cho killed 32 people and wounded 17 others before taking his own life.

There have been more than 365 mass shootings in the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting as an incident in which four or more people are shot, excluding the shooter.

articles.title: B.C. Conservatives drop candidate over post minimizing Holocaust
articles.summary: A B.C. Conservative candidate has been dropped after he was accused of posting offensive remarks on social media.

image.caption: Jordan McIntosh has been dropped as a B.C. Conservative candidate in Vancouver-Strathcona. (B.C. Conservative party website)

blocks.text: British Columbia
A B.C. Conservative candidate has been dropped after he was accused of posting offensive remarks on social media.
Jordan McIntosh dropped as the candidate for Vancouver-Strathcona
The party says Jordan McIntosh is no longer its candidate for Vancouver-Strathcona and that if elected, he will not sit in caucus.

The Conservatives announced his removal from the slate less than an hour after Callista Ryan, the NDP’s candidate for Vancouver-Quilchena, posted screenshots on social media platform X, showing what she said were McIntosh’s posts.
"Looks like Lorne Doerkson's candidate in Strathcona Jordan McIntosh thought he could use a nameless twitter account to say many awful, offensive things," Ryan said.
A post from an account linked to McIntosh repeated false claims that minimize aspects of the Holocaust.
The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs says they're glad the B.C. Conservatives acted quickly to remove McIntosh as a candidate.
Nico Slobinsky, the group's vice-president Pacific region, said on social media that the posts were "reprehensible and harmed our community by distorting the history of the Holocaust."
"Accountability matters for all seeking elected office," he said.
Ryan said the latest incident raises concerns about the Conservatives' vetting process.
"I see these comments as hateful, and that's something we absolutely have to call out and address."

McIntosh is a university student working toward a BA in geological engineering, according to his biography, which has since been removed from the party’s website. His LinkedIn page says he attends the University of Waterloo in Ontario.

A party spokesperson speaking on background says McIntosh was informed he was no longer a candidate shortly after Ryan's social media post. McIntosh is 18 years old and the party says it appears the posts were made when he was 15.
CBC News called a number listed as McIntosh's campaign number but it was not in service. It's unclear if McIntosh will run as an Independent.
The Vancouver-Strathcona riding was previously held by Joan Phillip, who died on Aug. 28.

items: B.C. Conservatives drop Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate after offensive social media posts

blocks.text: Amanda Burrows, who has served as director for First United in the Downtown Eastside, is the NDP’s candidate in that riding. It’s considered one of the safest NDP seats in the province.
This is the second time the B.C. Conservatives have dropped a candidate over offensive social media posts.
Last week, the party fired Joachim Agou in light of social media posts targeting Palestinians and Pakistanis that came to light.
B.C. Conservative Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate dropped after offensive posts
Doerkson has also faced calls from the Unified Muslim Associations of B.C. to drop Katy Merrifield as the party’s campaign director over anti-Islam posts.
Merrifield posted on X in June in response to a U.K. inquiry about child sexual exploitation: "F--k Islam. Defend Western civilization." The post was later removed.

items: B.C. Conservative campaign director under fire for anti-Islam posts

blocks.text: During Wednesday night's B.C. leaders' debate, Doerkson defended Merrifield, saying she is a sexual assault survivor who made the comments out of anger. Doerkson said she has since apologized and he will not remove her.
Doerkson hit back by accusing Eby of failing to stand up to antisemitism within the NDP, which led to the departure of former cabinet minister Selina Robinson.

items: Former cabinet minister Selina Robinson resigns from NDP caucus

blocks.text: The party did not make Doerkson available for an interview about McIntosh’s removal or the party's vetting process.
