articles.title: We know junk food isn't healthy, but scientists are trying to determine if it's also bad for our brains

image.caption: A new study co-authored by researchers form McMaster University suggest people who consume high amounts of ultra-processed foods in their diets may be at an increased likelihood of changes to their brain that could serve as precursors for stroke, dementia and cognitive decline. (Scott Olson/Getty Im

blocks.text: Most people have food in their fridges and cupboards that they know aren't the healthiest choice.

A box of chocolate chip cookies you grab for a bedtime snack. Instant noodles for when you can't be bothered to make dinner. Or that bag of ketchup chips you grabbed on a late night stroll home from the bar.

But it's not just guilty pleasures. Nearly half of the calories Canadians consume — 45.7 per cent on average, according to Statistics Canada — comes in the form of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and includes everything from breakfast cereals to frozen meals.
Over the years, research has shown that UPFs can negatively impact everything from our weight to our cardiovascular health, and could even be linked to some types of cancer.

items: What are the ultra-processed foods we eat and why does it matter to our health?

blocks.text: But a new study co-authored by two professors at Hamilton's McMaster University signals that our brains could also suffer as a result of consuming too many foods produced to be cheap and ready-to-eat.

The authors say that the people with the highest intake of UPFs in their diets may face an increased likelihood of experiencing changes to the brain that could serve as precursors for stroke, dementia and cognitive decline.
People wouldn't necessarily be aware of these potential harms, says study co-author Russell de Souza, an associate professor at McMaster's Mary Heersink School of Global Health and Social Medicine.
But he says the findings could encourage people to shift their eating habits now, before experiencing serious consequences later in life.
Why it can be hard to avoid ultra-processed foods
Feeding the furnace

De Souza and co-author Dr. Sonia Anand, a vascular medicine specialist, examined the diets and brain MRI scans of more than 8,700 Canadian adults, with a median age of about 58, and broke them down into four groups, from those with the lowest intake of UPFs to those with the highest.

The latter cohort was made up of people who consumed nearly 45 per cent of their calories from UPFs, or the equivalent of 16 servings a day, which they self-reported in a survey listing 150 to 170 food items consumer in the past year.
By comparison, the group with the lowest consumption got 15 per cent of their daily calories from UPFs, equal to three servings.

Anand, a professor of medicine and epidemiology at McMaster, says they analyzed the scans of higher-risk participants and found that their UPF-heavy diets were associated with increased body fat and visceral fat — the kind stored deeper in the body and around organs.
"Fat tissue in the wrong places can be almost like a furnace spewing out a whole bunch of inflammatory proteins that then affect our brains," she said.

Ultra-processed foods like instant noodles are mostly or entirely made from substances derived from plant and animal sources and combined with additives, preservatives, stabilizers, dyes and artificial flavours, rather than minimally-processed ingredients. (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)
Anand says the MRIs of the higher-risk group showed changes to the brain similar to silent strokes, a type of stroke that doesn't present any noticeable symptoms but damages the tissue.

These injuries add up over time and make it more likely that people could develop neurological problems, such as vascular dementia, says Dr. Michael Hill, a neurologist and professor at the University of Calgary who is not affiliated with the study.
"The more injuries you accumulate, the more likely you are to have neurological problems later in life, most commonly vascular dementia," he said.

items: Reducing ultra-processed food intake requires rethinking our 'food environment,' experts say
McMaster University study links ultra-processed food to range of health risks

blocks.text: While the damage a UPF-heavy diet may do can't be reversed, Hill says dietary changes can reduce further progression.
"Feed your brain," he said. "It's not just about your gut, right? It's about your whole body."
He says the findings are consistent with a growing body of evidence about the health impacts of UPFs.
LISTEN | About 1/3 of Canadian adults are obese. Ultra-processed foods are a major culprit:
The Dose21:34What's the harm in eating ultra-processed foods and what can I do about it?
'Eat foods that rot, not rotten foods'
De Souza notes that not all processed foods are ultra-processed and, in fact, many processed products in grocery stores have a lot of nutritional value.
"Some degree of processing is absolutely necessary in the food supply," he said. "It helps keep food safe and shelf stable."
But a can of beans, a bag of frozen vegetables or a container of yogurt are all different from a fast-food meal or a box of sugar-coated cereal.

Foods are classified using what's known as the NOVA system, where foods are determined to be ultra-processed if they are mostly or entirely made from substances derived from plant and animal sources and combined with additives like salt, sugar, fats and oils, as well as preservatives, stabilizers, dyes and artificial flavours.
They also tend to be lower in fibre, vitamins and minerals that benefit overall health, de Souza says.

items: What would it take for Canadians to eat less ultra-processed foods?

blocks.text: Hill says that while "one Snickers bar isn't going to hurt you," ultimately, ultra-processed food isn't going to benefit your health — especially if you're eating it regularly.
And even when people want a sugary or salty treat, he says it's going to be better if they make it at home from whole or minimally-processed foods.
"Eat foods that will rot, but not rotten food," he said.

Anand and de Souza note that their study doesn't provide the full picture of the potential toll UPFs can have on brain health and say more long-term research is needed to determine if dietary changes later in life can make a difference.

The next phase of their research will see 2,000 people who took part in the first round of scans receive a second round to determine if reducing the amount of UPFs in their diets results in changes or improvements to brain health.
5 tips on how to eat fewer ultra-processed foods
Improving health literacy

Anand notes that not everyone has the time or money to prepare high-quality food, which she says is a systemic issue that would require government intervention to reduce the amount of UPFs available and make healthy food more affordable.
It's also a matter of improving health literacy, which she says would increase awareness about the repercussions of consuming too many UPFs.

items: Nutrition warning labels are hitting shelves near you — earlier than expected

blocks.text: Canada, she says, could follow the lead of other countries that have successfully minimized the consumption of UPFs. One such country, Chile, implemented mandatory front-of-package labels for UPFs that are high in sugar in an effort to curb childhood obesity.
She says there are things individuals and governments can do "and we need both to happen to make Canadians healthier."
Plant-based ultra-processed foods raise risk of heart disease and death, study suggests

articles.title: Milei adviser claims UK being ‘colonised by Islam’ as Falklands row grows
articles.summary:
Santiago Caputo cites election of Sagal Abdi-Wali as MP and calls UK a threat to the west in post shared by Argentina’s president

The chief adviser to Argentina’s president, Javier Milei,…
articles.byline: Daniel Boffey in Port Stanley, Falkland Islands

blocks.text: The chief adviser to Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has cited the election of Sagal Abdi-Wali to the UK parliament as evidence of the Islamisation of Britain and further reason for Argentina to take sovereignty over the Falkland Islands.

In a post on social media, Santiago Caputo, who is reportedly taking a key role in Argentina’s strategy over the Falklands, suggested that the taking of the south Atlantic islands was necessary to prevent the “interference of an Islamic state” in the region.
Milei shared Caputo’s on the social media platform X.

The intervention from Buenos Aires comes at a moment of heightened tension between Argentina and the UK over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory, which is 300 miles off the South American coastline.
Labour’s Abdi-Wali was elected as the MP for Holborn and St Pancras in London this month, seeing off a challenge from the Green party leader, Zack Polanski. She took her seat in parliament on Monday.
Milei has sought to criminalise executives involved in the Falkland Islands’ nascent oil industry and has threatened to target the fishing sector on which the islands’ economy depends.

Argentina has long sought sovereignty over the islands. The intensity of Argentinian pressure relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by the then Argentinian dictator, Gen Leopoldo Galtieri.

blocks.caption: Javier Milei shared his adviser’s post on X. Photograph: Francisco Loureiro/Reuters

blocks.text: The 74-day conflict in 1982 ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of their military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders.

This week, Andy Burnham restated the UK’s position that it would respect the wish of the 3,600 islanders to remain British, and the government announced its intention to protect the interests of businesses working in the Falklands.

The Guardian revealed that the Foreign Office had written to Interpol seeking assurance that the law enforcement agency would not respond favourably to requests for the detention of individuals working in the Falklands.

In his statement on X, Caputo – who has worked for Milei since 2021 – wrote that the “United Kingdom was, in many ways, the cradle of modern western civilisation” but that it now posed a threat to the west.

He wrote: “Seeing the United Kingdom being colonised by Islam is not only an imminent risk to the cause of the west as a whole, but also a historical tragedy for those of us who defend the ideas of liberty.

“This is yet another reason why Argentina must firmly project itself toward the south Atlantic and reclaim the Las Malvinas [Argentina’s name for the Falklands]. Given the strategic geopolitical importance the south Atlantic will assume in the coming decades, the west cannot afford the encroachment of an Islamic state within that sphere of influence. Reclaiming the Malvinas is not merely a national cause, it is a cause for the west.”
Caputo accompanied his post with an image of Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee from Somalia, being sworn into parliament.

Under the image, Javier Negre, a rightwing Spanish journalist, commented: “Here is a Somali Muslim woman taking her oath of office on the Qur’an in the English parliament. She has taken the seat formerly held by Prime Minister Keir Starmer. Islam is steadily gaining more power in the country.”
In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of the Falkland Islands’ residents voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.

articles.title: Was Neanderthal life violent? This wound suggests lethal fighting was more common
articles.summary: A 75,000-year-old Neanderthal spear wound may be evidence violence shaped human life far earlier than thought.

blocks.text: A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been struck through the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, archaeologists say.
They say a 15mm hole found in a shoulder blade in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan could be the earliest evidence of lethal violence involving such a weapon.

From the angle of the wound and other evidence, the researchers believe the spear entered the individual's chest and passed through the body - probably damaging a lung and major blood vessels - and exited through the left shoulder blade to leave a near-perfect hole.
The research is the latest in emerging evidence that suggests Neanderthal societies experienced more violence than previously thought.

Neanderthals were a separate species of humans that went extinct around 40,000 years ago. They lived across a large expanse of Europe and western and central Asia, and sometimes overlapped with our species, Homo sapiens.
The wounded Neanderthal's remains were found in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. As well as the left shoulder blade, the individual's right hand, three ribs and some teeth were also found.

A hole in the shoulder blade may be the earliest evidence of "lethal interpersonal violence" from a wooden spear, according to Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology.
"The fatal strike may have been an intended heart shot," she told BBC News.
Archaeologists call the remains Shanidar A, named after the cave in which they were found. Remains of at least 10 Neanderthals were discovered in excavations in the cave in the 1950s.
The wound is thought to be the first evidence for use of sharpened wooden spears in the prehistoric Middle East, according to Pomeroy.
"It is not the kind of break that you would get naturally, because it is so circular," she said. "Experiments with reconstructed wooden spears produce very similar round holes in bone."
But the interpersonal violence is by no means certain, she says. It may be a case of friendly fire, a wound caused as a result of a hunting accident.
But Prof Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum in London, who was not involved in the research, told BBC News that an attack by a rival was the more plausible explanation.

"The researchers leave it open whether this resulted from a hunting accident or interpersonal violence, but in my view the latter seems more likely, given the positioning and extent of the wound," he said.

This discovery has echoes of an earlier find in the same cave, in 1957. Those remains involved another Neanderthal who lived more recently, around 50, 000 years ago. Their ribs had evidence of a partly healed wound, which archaeologists believe was probably caused by a stone-tipped spear.

We can't tell for sure whether these Neanderthals were hurt by a companion during a hunt or murdered by a rival. But they join a small but growing body of evidence which point to the possibility that human-on-human violence was more common and goes back further than the current scientific consensus would suggest.
"I unfortunately see the growing body of evidence as an indication that interpersonal violence goes deep into human prehistory," Stringer told BBC News.

A key piece of that evidence is a study published in 2022 of very early Neanderthal skulls from northern Spain at an archaeological site called "the Pit of Bones". It suggests that deadly violence was taking place about 430,000 years ago.

Researchers found 57 healed head injuries among 20 individuals. Nine individuals had potentially fatal skull fractures. Six had similar puncture wounds at the back-left of the head. Because the wounds repeatedly occurred in almost the same place, the researchers concluded that deliberate blows were more likely than accidental damage. One skull had two wounds that had probably been inflicted with the same object.

The Pit of Bones findings do not show that everyone in this population was habitually violent, but they provide strong evidence that repeated killing occurred among these people hundreds of thousands of years ago.
For decades, many archaeologists linked the beginnings of organised warfare to farming, when people began living in permanent settlements and competing over land, livestock and food stores.
But evidence from earlier hunter-gatherers and still older human relatives has since shown that individual killings pre-date farming by a very long way.
The live scientific debate is over how common such violence was, and when sporadic attacks became organised conflict and wars between groups.
The research has been published in the journal Scientific Reports.

articles.title: How long can shelter animals be left alone overnight? B.C. advocates want a limit written in law
articles.summary: A North Vancouver man's report of a dog crying through the night at a local animal shelter has ignited a push from pet advocates to write into law how long shelter animals can be left alone.

image.caption: Luna was found abandoned in Lynn Valley on Sept. 3 and taken to the District of North Vancouver animal shelter, where a nearby resident heard her crying through the nights. (Submitted by the District of North Vancouver)

blocks.text: British Columbia
A North Vancouver man's report of a dog crying through the night at a local animal shelter has ignited a push from pet advocates to write into law how long shelter animals can be left alone.
Shelters say animals are unattended at night, sometimes for more than 16 hours
Those concerns came into focus in late September, when Daniel Weidner posted online about hearing a dog, named Luna, crying overnight at a local animal shelter for more than a week.
"It was midnight all the way through until 6 or 7 a.m.," Weidner told CBC News, after posting about Luna on Facebook.

While B.C.’s Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act (PCA) requires people responsible for animals to protect them from distress, it doesn't set a maximum length of time that shelter animals can be left without staff on site.
That leaves staffing decisions to local shelters.
But some advocates want clearer rules and more oversight from the province.
Weidner’s post drew 10 more residents to the District of North Vancouver’s animal shelter that weekend, some offering to foster or adopt Luna, and others demanding the dog's release.

After Weidner, far left, posted about a dog crying at the District of North Vancouver's animal shelter, a group of residents, including Bunting, third from left, expressed their concern by showing up to the shelter on Sept. 27. (Submitted by Daniel Weidner)

One was Kelly Bunting, a volunteer dog walker at the B.C. SPCA’s West Vancouver centre, who filed a complaint after learning the senior dog she walked there, Clyde, was left without staff on site from 5 p.m. until 8 a.m.

"It was just breaking my heart when I would take him for a walk, then I would put him back in his kennel … I knew he was going to be in there until the next day. I couldn’t sleep and I couldn’t stop thinking about him," she said.
The standards
Several animal shelters in B.C. told CBC News they don’t have staff scheduled on site overnight, with those periods ranging from roughly 10 hours to more than 16 hours.

In separate emails to CBC News, the District of North Vancouver said staff at its animal shelter typically leave around 5 p.m. and return between 8 and 9:30 a.m., while the B.C. SPCA confirmed staff are scheduled at its West Vancouver centre from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
The B.C. SPCA also said in an email, "generally speaking" all its centres — a total of 37, according to its website — have staff on site for between eight and nine hours a day.
The B.C. SPCA and the district told CBC News Clyde and Luna have since been adopted.
A senior dog named Clyde stayed at the B.C. SPCA's West Vancouver centre for seven weeks, according to the society. (Submitted by Kelly Bunting)
Both Bunting and Weidner want to see change.
Bunting said she hopes the province will write into law that shelter animals can't be left unattended for more than 12 hour.
Weidner, meanwhile, has called for a top-to-bottom review of the North Vancouver shelter's operations and policies around how animals are cared for.
The district wrote in an email that dogs in its care meet accepted standards used by shelters in the region.
The B.C. SPCA says its care standards meet and often exceed recommendations in the Association of Shelter Veterinarians guidelines, generally considered the benchmark of care in North America.
In Canada, animal shelters adopt best practices rather than rely on legal requirements, according to Maneesha Deckha, an animal law professor at the University of Victoria.

Those best practices, she said, are not always enforceable and often rely on goodwill, which is why she believes requirements for on-site staffing should be regulated by "animal-centred" law, valuing animals as relational beings.
What can change?
Rebecca Ledger, an animal welfare and behaviour scientist, said 15 hours alone can be tolerable for some dogs, but may cause stress for others.
She reviewed recordings Weidner took of Luna and said it sounded like a dog trying to get attention.
Ledger said most shelters are aware of issues that come with prolonged confinement, particularly overnight, but "many simply don’t have the resources to provide more care than they already do."
According to animal lawyer Victoria Shroff, the issue doesn't start at the shelter level, but with the lack of robust laws and systems in place.
She said it is "incumbent on the provincial government" to better fund animal welfare, and hopes the next government will form a task force to address gaps in care.
Provincial parties respond
The province said it would not comment while the provincial election is underway.
CBC News reached out to all five major provincial political parties and asked how, if elected, their governments would address concerns around staff supervision at animal shelters.

A spokesperson for the B.C. Conservatives said its government would work with the B.C. SPCA and municipalities to set enforceable standards, "including how long [shelter animals] can go without supervision."
CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko wrote in an email that her party would conduct a review of the province's current animal welfare legislation, to strengthen laws and properly protect shelter animals.
The B.C. NDP, the B.C. Greens and OneBC did not respond by deadline.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Arden McLeod, from Vancouver, is an associate producer with CBC News. He has a passion for community storytelling, local news, and reflecting the values of B.C. He graduated from the British Columbia Institute of Technology's broadcast and online journalism program. You can reach him at Arden.McLeod@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Trump calls off livestream for Fort Hood shooter's execution by firing squad
articles.summary: Trump said some would "rather not watch" the execution of Nidal Hasan, the first military execution in over 60 years.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.
Trump had previously said he approved of showing online the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it.
As criticism over the public display mounted, Trump said on Thursday that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die".
"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said.
"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added.
Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at a military base in Texas in 2009, injuring another 32. His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.
Trump said the execution can be viewed in person by the families of the victims.
"They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" Trump said.

articles.title: Can Kenya preserve the democratic space Raila Odinga fought for?
articles.summary: One year after the former prime minister's death, Kenyans are reflecting on his contribution to democracy and national reconciliation. Odinga's "handshakes" with his political rivals remain the…

image.caption: Raila Odinga continues to influence Kenya's political discourse even after his deathImage: Simon Maina/AFP

blocks.text: AsKenya marks the first anniversary of Raila Odinga's death on Thursday, the former prime minister remains a towering figure. For many, he symbolizes the struggle for multiparty democracyand constitutional reforms. For others, his political alliances raise questions about compromise, opposition politics and the direction of the movement he built.

The question is not only how Kenya remembers Odinga — but whether the principles he championed can survive. "I want his legacy to live beyond the party," 20-year-old Nairobi resident Beatrice Chebet told DW.
Chebet said Odinga wanted a Kenya grounded in peace, democracy, constitutionalism and the rule of law. She said younger generations must carry those aspirations forward.

blocks.caption: Odinga was fondly referred to as "Baba," or father, by his supportersImage: Halima Gongo/DW

blocks.text: Odinga had a lasting effect on the experiences and political journey of younger Kenyans, Chebet said. "Some of us were Gen Zs," she said. "We did not know any form of multipartyism without reading Raila.”
Forged in struggle

Odinga's influence was shaped by decades of opposition politics, detentions and campaigns for democratic change. His role in the disputed 2007 presidential election placed him at the center of one of Kenya's most consequential political crises. The postelection violence killed more than 1,100 people and displaced hundreds of thousands.

A power-sharing agreement brokered with international mediation led by Kofi Annan, the former secretary-general of the United Nations, made Odinga prime minister in a coalition government with President Mwai Kibaki. The settlement also established a reform agenda, including constitutional change. Kenya adopted a new constitution in 2010, introducing a devolved system of government.

The security and intelligence strategist Byron Adera said Odinga's impact extended beyond electoral politics. "Raila was an institution that rocked institutions, bringing about lasting and very impactful institutional reforms for the betterment of Kenya," Adera told DW. He identifies constitutional reform and efforts to bring competing political interests together as important parts of Odinga's legacy.
A look at the life of Kenya's Raila Odinga

Reconciliation also became one of the most contested aspects of Odinga's career. His "handshakes" of reconciliation with Kibaki in 2008 and President Uhuru Kenyatta in 2018 and cooperation with President William Ruto in 2024 illustrated his willingness to pursue political agreements with former rivals.

Supporters saw dialogue as a way to reduce tensions and advance national interests; critics questioned what such arrangements meant for an independent opposition. Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has strongly criticized the political rapprochement between President William Ruto and the late Raila Odinga.

In May, Gachagua called the handshake process "nonsense" and said it had eroded Kenya's democracy by weakening the opposition's ability to hold the government accountable. His position offers a contrasting view of the alliances that shaped Odinga's later political years.
What happens to Odinga's ODM party?
The debate over Odinga's legacy is especially pressing within the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), the party he helped found and led for years.

Edwin Sifuna, a potential presidential candidate in the 2027 election, who describes Odinga as both his leader and friend, said the ODM's identity and direction had changed fundamentally. "We run the risk of losing our core support, people who believed in the ideals of ODM, because we were always the party of the people," Sifuna told DW.

Sifuna said Odinga's influence on national politics and public debate was greatly missed. His remarks point to a central challenge for ODM: whether it can preserve its identity and connection with ordinary Kenyans while navigating a changing political landscape. However, in a bid to keep the Odinga name in politics, Winnie Odinga, daughter of Raila Odinga, declared that she will run for Senator of Nairobi County in the 2027 election.

Chebet said Odinga's legacy would be measured by whether future generations continue to defend the principles associated with his political journey. Adera, meanwhile, emphasizes the lasting importance of institutional reform and building bridges.

Their perspectives highlight the tension at the heart of Odinga's legacy: a leader remembered for expanding democratic possibilities, but whose political compromises remain debatable. A year after his death, Odinga's influence is still visible in Kenya's political arguments, party divisions and public calls for democratic accountability.

The lasting test will be whether Kenya's institutions, political parties and younger generation can carry those principles forward — and whether the democratic space Odinga helped shape can endure beyond the man himself.

articles.title: Resources minister faces calls to correct her claim all Beetaloo emissions will be offset
articles.summary: Madeleine King told press club emissions from NT fossil fuel basin ‘are accounted for and offset’ but research found 95% of emissions this decade would not have to be offset
articles.byline: Adam Morton and Sarah Basford Canales

blocks.text: The resources minister, Madeleine King, is facing calls to correct her claim in a major speech that all greenhouse gas emissions from developing a massive fossil fuel basin in the Northern Territory will be offset to limit their impact on the climate.

Speaking at the National Press Club in Canberra on Wednesday, King defended her support for the development of the Beetaloo gas basin south of Darwin after being asked if she was comfortable with the impact that the emissions from the gas would have on Australians.

King was photographed laughing alongside the NT chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro, as they celebrated the first gas being pumped from the basin last month. The minister told the press club the basin was a “very important resource” for the NT and to help supply gas to Australia’s east coast and export markets.

She said it was being developed after a “landmark scientific study” in 2018 into whether fracking should be allowed in the territory. Known as the Pepper inquiry, that government-commissioned investigation made 135 recommendations, including that the NT and Australian governments should aim to ensure that any onshore shale gas developments did not increase the country’s total emissions.
In practice, that would require any climate pollution from gas developments – from extraction, processing, transport and the fuel’s use – to be fully offset through the purchase of carbon credits.

King told the press club that the NT government “took up and implemented” the inquiry’s recommendations. “My understanding from those recommendations is that the emissions are accounted for and offset, but I would have to check that,” she said.

The NT government does not require emissions from Beetaloo basin to be offset. The Guardian revealed that the previous Labor territory government dropped the requirement after the gas industry objected. The Country Liberal party government maintained that position when elected in 2024.

Some emissions from gas developments in the NT will need to be offset under a federal climate policy, the safeguard mechanism, that is applied to operations that emit more than 100,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. But that applies only to pollution directly from the facility, not the full lifecycle emissions as recommended by the Pepper inquiry.

King told the press club the safeguard mechanism would be applied to Beetaloo basin developments if emissions were above the threshold. “That is how we manage dealing with emissions in this country,” she said.
But research by Tim Baxter, of the consultancy Naru Research, found about 95% of emissions expected from four gas projects in the Beetaloo basin this decade would not have to be offset.
Baxter said King either “isn’t across her brief or she’s being intentionally misleading”.
after newsletter promotion
“The Pepper inquiry was clear. For the territory to begin to manage the risks of fracking and unconventional gas in the NT all emissions occurring in Australia must be fully offset,” he said.
“The safeguard mechanism does not deliver this … If NT fracking is detonated, it could single-handedly undo all efforts to cut Australia’s climate emissions.”

Kirsty Howey, a former head of Environment Centre NT, now leading the Wilderness Society, said governments had broken a promise to fully act on the recommendations of the Pepper inquiry. “It’s one of the greatest failures of climate policy in history,” she said.

The acting chief head of Environment Centre NT, Bree Ahrens, called on the minister to “correct the public record”. She said an estimate by the energy company Santos suggested if the Beetaloo basin was fully developed and its gas burned it could lead to emissions 60 times what Australia releases into the atmosphere each year.
“Frackers are being given a free pass on climate emissions, and it’s the territory that will pay the price,” she said.

A spokesperson for King said successive NT governments had “accepted and implemented all 135 recommendations of the Pepper review”. They said the safeguard mechanism required all shale gas facilities, including Beetaloo basin gas extraction facilities, to have net zero emissions if they emitted more than 100,000 tonnes of CO2 a year.

articles.title: Queensland’s LNP has tread softly in government. It’s now baring its teeth over the power to break up workers’ strikes
articles.summary:
The controversial legislation may end up placing large sections of its suburban support – critical to the party’s lead in the polls – on the bonfire

  • Get our

blocks.text: For almost two years, the Liberal National party’s strategy for government in Queensland has been to stay well clear of issues that risk burning through political capital.
On Wednesday, one of the most tentative conservative governments in recent history announced plans for sweeping and controversial changes to workplace laws.
In doing so, the LNP risks placing large sections of its suburban support – critical to the party’s lead in the polls – on the bonfire.

The proposals would give the increasingly influential deputy premier, Jarrod Bleijie, the power to break strikes by public sector workers in certain circumstances, including if it is deemed “in the public interest”.

The government will also make it more difficult for public servants, including emergency services workers, to claim compensation for psychological injuries. Under the proposed laws, workers with such claims will only be entitled to support if they can show their workplace was the primary cause.

Law firm Slater and Gordon said the changes would make it harder for Queenslanders to access support for psychological injuries. The United Workers Union, which represents paramedics and some healthcare workers, said the changes were “an underhanded attack on Queensland ambulance officers and other hospital staff”.
Several business groups welcomed the changes.

The opposition leader, Steven Miles, said on Thursday morning the proposals were a “Newman-era attack on workers”, and the only thing surprising about that statement was that it took so long (roughly 14 hours) for the spectre of Campbell Newman’s government to, once again, loom over Queensland politics.

The collapse of the Newman government explains almost everything about the current one. The premier, David Crisafulli, and Bleijie had front-row seats for the “crash through” tactics that quickly turned voters off Newman, including proposals to sack public sector workers, and led to mass protests.

The lessons since have been that most suburban voters are uncomfortable with the LNP putting ideology on show. And so it went to the 2024 election – and won comfortably – talking mainly about crime and keeping all those vote-losing positions on things like abortion and budget cuts off the table.
Approaching the midway point of the term, the LNP has finally decided to show its teeth.
There are readers who will, understandably, take issue with the idea that the Crisafulli government has been “tentative” or has been, up to this point, unthreatening.
It has been unapologetic in attacking Indigenous representation within government, trans healthcare, and suppressing pro-Palestine protests.
These moves have been underpinned by a simple calculation: that the issues are marginal for most suburban and regional voters, whose concerns are mostly the cost of living and crime.

Those who care about evidence-based policy, human rights and civil liberties have every right to be furious. The polls suggest that fury hasn’t gone mainstream, and that suburban voters are OK with the government punching down, so long as it doesn’t affect them.
after newsletter promotion

Workplace reforms affect them. If nothing else, those survivors of the Newman government who still sit in the cabinet room will have learned a lesson that in Queensland, the public sector (which employs more than 320,000 people) is a powerful political bloc in its own right.
The morning after announcing the changes, Bleijie seemed only too aware of the scale of the coming fight.
“You’re going to see a mammoth campaign by the Labor party,” he told reporters at a press conference at Newstead.
“It’s going to be a lot of mistruths and misinformation, and I think everything they will be able to say … we will be able to debunk with facts.”

The Crisafulli government remains comfortably ahead in the relatively few public polls, a recent snapshot in Brisbane Times seemed to show Labor in Queensland had taken the biggest hit from the rise in support for One Nation.

But the bright orange cloud is still looming. And a simple look around the country reveals that in modern times, whether policy is decided by ideology or focus group, there’s no guarantee political capital will last.
Better use that capital while you can. Even if it means, as it will for the Queensland LNP, picking a fight with many of the suburban middle-class voters who put the party into office.

items: Ben Smee is Queensland state correspondent

articles.title: Resignation of Bärbel Bas shines light on harsh era of German politics
articles.summary: German Labor Minister Bärbel Bas has stepped down, citing her need to grieve a loved one and leave behind the harsh realities of government. So how did German politics get so heated?

image.caption: Bas (right) stepped down following criticism from Merz (left)Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: For a brief moment, a sense of quiet sympathy could be felt in Berlin's often unforgiving political arena: On Monday morning, Bärbel Bas, Germany's labor minister and the co-leader of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) announced her resignation from all government and party positions. The 58-year-old politician cited a personal tragedy as the reason for her decision: "Following the death of my stepdaughter, I have come to realize that I need time to work through my grief," Bas wrote in a statement.

Bas also wrote that sustained criticism from the conservative governing parties, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU), had contributed to her decision to step down. In her statement, she wrote that she had been forced to "conclude that public attacks on me, unfortunately also from within the ranks of our coalition partner, continued to intensify during this personally difficult time."

The labor minister had recently been responsible for implementing complex changes to Germany's public pension system — including increasing the retirement age — and had been urged by some conservative politicians, in rather harsh terms, not to delay the project any further.

According to a report in the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, one remark in particular appears to have weighed heavily on her: During an off-the-record briefing with journalists, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, of the CDU, reportedly criticized the pace of her efforts despite knowing that she was working through a personal tragedy.
Did Bas feel so overwhelmed by pressures both personal and political that she chose to step down rather than continue to endure them?

Mirco Liefke, a researcher with the Institute for Media and Communication Studies in the Department of Political and Social Sciences at the Freie Universität Berlin, told DW that unfairness and harshness have always been part of politics. However, he added: "What I do think is new is the potential for escalation and the speed that social media have brought to public debate. Along with that has come an incentive for individual actors to adopt ever more radical positions."

blocks.caption: Bas (right) was asked to implement increases to the retirement ageImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Politics and media

There are few public spaces left in which politicians can speak with the expectation that their remarks will not be reported. Merz is said to have made critical remarks of Bas during an off-the-record briefing whose contents were not intended for publication.
Though he was fully aware of her personal circumstances, Merz reportedly said Bas was barely visible in public and failing to put forward proposals of her own.
"It has effectively become a business model to leak information that is meant to remain confidential and thereby generate attention," Liefke said.
A spokesperson for Merz declined to confirm or deny the report.
Politics and misogyny

Felix Banaszak, the co-leader of Germany's center-left Greens, has known Bas fior years, with both hailing from Duisburg, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, albeit born a couple of decades apart.
"Toughness and ruthlessness are nothing new in politics," Banaszak told DW. "But we still need to find a different way of doing things if we do not want to keep wearing people down."

Banaszak said the SPD was partially responsible for the treatment of Bas. "The fact that Bärbel Bas encountered so little understanding for her personal situation from within the ranks of the coalition partner, and that apparently no one in the SPD was willing to step forward, defend her, and take her out of the line of fire, is simply not a good sign," he said.
"It would be naive to pretend that the attacks on a man would have unfolded in a similar way," he added.
Liefke offered a similar view: "Women politicians are subjected to an extraordinary degree of misogynistic and sexualized abuse — and they face a level of public exposure that is entirely new."
CDU pushes back

The debate over how Bas and her grief should have been treated soon took on some of the same characteristics as the attacks that had preceded her resignation. Manuela Schwesig, the SPD state premier of the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, described the attacks by the CDU/CSU as "inhuman," drawing sharp criticism from many conservative politicians. Merz publicly expressed his regret over the labor minister's resignation and wished her all the best.

Liefke said this was another tremnd in German politics. Once a politician decides to step down, he argues, public expressions of concern are often far more intense than they used to be and come from all sides: "This is a facade of concern," he said. "There is something ritualistic, almost reflexive, about it. People react this way because they are following another major trend: Emotionalization."

blocks.caption: Kühnert cited far-right threats in his resignation as SPD general secretaryImage: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The case of Kevin Kühnert

The attacks on Bas are just one example of the increasingly harsh tone of political debate. Formal reprimands in the Bundestag have risen sharply, particularly since the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) entered parliament in 2017. High-profile resignations have also made headlines, including that of Kevin Kühnert, the SPD's former secretary-general.

Kühnert stepped down in 2024, citing health reasons. In April 2025, however, he told Die Zeit newspaper that he had felt constantly threatened by far-right extremists. Political debate, he said, is showing "an increasing lack of respect for the views of those who think differently."

blocks.caption: Helmut Schmidt managed to maintain his private life throughout his chancellorshipImage: picture alliance / ASSOCIATED PRESS

blocks.text: Former Chancellor Helmut Schmidt: A public figure, yet still private

Liefke points out that politicians once managed to maintain two distinct modes of communication: One public and one private. "When you think of earlier generations of politicians, what comes to mind is the distance they maintained, the relative lack of emotional display. Take Helmut Schmidt, for example. He did not openly grieve over things that came crashing down on him. At least, he did not show it publicly." Helmut Schmidt, of the SPD, served as chancellor from 1974 to 1982.

Liefke argues: "Today, politicians such as Bärbel Bas benefit from drawing on their own life stories when they say, 'I come from a working-class background and worked my way up.' That can work to their advantage, but it also makes them far more visible, and far more vulnerable, as individuals."

Bas, who served as president of the Bundestag from 2021 to 2025, intends to retain her parliamentary seat. Life is likely to become quieter for her now, while others move into the spotlight, both in public and, perhaps, in private as well.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Hamburg court jails 2 men over plot to attack Jewish leaders on behalf of Iran
articles.summary: The pair was found guilty of espionage and attempted murder. The court says they planned to attack the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany and president of the German-Israeli society.

image.caption: The men were sentenced in Hamburg after being extradited from Denmark [FILE: October 3, 2020]Image: xim.gs/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A Hamburg court on Thursday sentenced two men accused of plotting to target Jewish leaders in Germany on behalf of Iran'ssecret service to multiple years in prison.

Both were found guilty of espionage and attempted murder. One defendant was given a four-and-a-half year sentence, while the other received an eight-and-a-half year sentence as the mastermind of the planned attacks.
Prosecutors said that one defendant, a 54-year-old Dane with Afghan roots, had received his orders directly from Iran's al-Quds Brigades, the foreign arm of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.
The man was said to have recruited his accomplice, a 43-year-old Afghan man living in Denmark, to carry out one of the attacks, or find someone who could.
The 43-year-old was also tasked with finding a weapon with which to carry out one of the attacks.
Beyond targeting two high-profile individuals, the 54-year-old had reportedly made preparations for an arson attack on a kosher deli in Berlin.
The defendants were arrested by Danish authorities in the city of Aarhus last year and extradited to Germany.
How Europe, the US can better protect Jewish communities
Who were convicted defendants planning to attack?
Among the figures the pair planned to attack was Josef Schuster, the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, the court found.
Another prospective target was Green Party politician Volker Beck, president of the German-Israeli society.
Beck called on Berlin to expel Iran's ambassador and consular officials after charges against the men were made public.
"Jewish life and a commitment to the Jewish and democratic state are repeatedly threatened with murder and attacked by the regime of the Islamic Republic of Iran on German soil," he said.

Germany's Foreign Office summoned Iran's ambassador after Danish authorities made the arrests, prompting the Iranian embassy in Berlin to release a statement rejecting what it called "unfounded allegations made at the behest of Iran's enemies."

articles.title: DSWD urges content creators to be respectful of PWDs
articles.summary: The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) told content creators to be more respectful of people with mental health conditions.

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 9:37pm

Every individual with a disability, including those on the autism spectrum or with neurodevelopmental conditions, deserves dignity, respect, privacy, and the utmost care, DSWD said. (Photo from DSWD FB post)
The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) told content creators to be more respectful of people with mental health conditions.
The agency issued the statement in response to a viral incident wherein the hosts of the podcast Machong Chismisan made fun of people on the autism spectrum.

"Every individual with a disability, including those on the autism spectrum or with neurodevelopmental conditions, deserves dignity, respect, privacy, and the utmost care. Exploiting a person's disability for amusement, ridicule, or online engagement is unacceptable, as it reinforces harmful stereotypes and drives discrimination against a vulnerable group," DSWD spokesperson Assistant Secretary Irene Dumlao said.

"We urge all content creators to exercise responsibility in discussing topics that make fun and violate the rights of vulnerable sectors such as persons with disabilities, whether it is apparent or non-apparent. We need to protect their dignity not only as an act of compassion but also as part of upholding their human rights," she added.
Dumlao said that content creators have the responsibility of fostering inclusive digital spaces and ensuring that they are mindful of the rights of vulnerable people.
The DSWD said that under the Magna Carta for Persons with Disabilities, any act that shames, ridicules, or vilifies a person with disabilities is punishable under the law.
While the agency did not name names, the controversial episode of Machong Chismisan poked fun at Josh Aquino, the son of media personality Kris Aquino.
The hosts of the show have since apologized and taken down the episode following the backlash. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: AI-assisted dying? Doris Dörrie's new film addresses prospect of care robots
articles.summary: While the world debates the dangers of artificial intelligence, filmmaker Doris Dörrie explores how humanoid robots could change the way we deal with aging, caregiving and how people choose to die.

image.caption: A care robot named Pavlovich takes over the care of Mrs. WinklerImage: Mathias Bothor/Zeitsprung Pictures/Wild Bunch Germany/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hamburg in the near future: Instead of human drivers, robots deliver parcels. In cafes, robots roll between the tables, serving diners. On the streets, one encounters humanoid robots walking dogs — or the other way around, people taking their robot dogs for a walk.

This is the setting of Doris Dörrie's new film, "Frau Winkler verlässt das Haus" ("Mrs. Winkler Leaves the House"). At the core of the plot is an elderly woman who can no longer live on her own after a fall. With her only daughter unable to provide permanent care, the solution seems simple enough: a care robot with a built-in EOL program, or "End of Life" mode. This robot not only assists with everyday life but can also provide assisted dying under certain conditions, namely when the person explicitly wishes to end their life and meets the relevant medical criteria.

Dörrie's film tackles several major social issues with remarkable lightness. These include the challenges facing aging societies such as Germany, Japan and China, the question of dying on one's own terms and a mother-daughter relationship that raises questions of guilt and responsibility. Even though the story is set in Germany, such issues resonate globally.
"I write about what personally moves and interests me," Dörrie told DW.

One of the best-known contemporary German film directors, Dörrie achieved her breakthrough in 1985 with the comedy "Men…" She gained further international recognition with films such as 2008's "Cherry Blossoms" and "Greetings from Fukushima" (2016).
Who decides when we die?

Assisted suicide is one of the most complex ethical questions of our time. Laws vary around the world. Though some countries permit active euthanasia under certain conditions, others prohibit and criminalize all forms of assisted dying.
What is assisted suicide and where does Germany stand?
In her film, Dörrie asks what happens when artificial intelligence begins calculating the cost of caring for an elderly person and weighing whether that cost is still "worth" bearing for society.

The underlying idea isn't new, Dörrie said, pointing to the Japanese legend of Narayama, which is also mentioned in the film. According to the legend, the eldest children were responsible for taking their ageing parents to a mountain and leaving them there to die because there was not enough food for everyone. "And that's also the debate we are currently facing to a certain extent: Can we really afford to let older people live longer and longer?"

In Dörrie's film, elderly people are allowed to make their own decisions once they reach a certain state of health — but they can't change their minds afterwards. Yet what does it really mean to make a decision freely? "It's a tricky situation," says Dörrie, because the question is to what extent one is also pressured into making this decision, "not only because it makes more economic sense, but also because one is no longer a burden on one's loved ones — in this case, one's daughter..."

The film often raises these questions indirectly and with plenty of dark humor. At one point, a care adviser presents the EOL feature to Mrs. Winkler as an attractive and, above all, straightforward additional option, making it sound as though there would be nothing more for her to worry about.

blocks.caption: Doris Dörrie (left) with actors Angela Winkler and Laura TonkeImage: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Staying close despite the algorithm

Dörrie is not interested in demonizing AI in her film — quite the opposite. In the film, the care robot, which Mrs. Winkler names Pavlovich, helps the elderly woman rediscover some of her zest for life and get out of the house.

"When you travel through Germany, you see small houses everywhere, and statistics show that an elderly person lives alone in every other house," Dörrie said. "If AI can help in these circumstances, why not use it?" She said she sought to explore this ambiguity in her film. Dividing things into black and white would neither be interesting nor, in her view, accurate.

Dörrie and her crew were surprised during filming by how quickly people can develop emotional bonds with robots. She attributes this to the human brain. "We regard anything that moves and speaks as a living being. We can't help it," she explains. And that is precisely what we need to pay attention to when interacting with AI, Dörrie says. "How often are we truly aware that we are talking to a machine rather than a living being? These are things we still have to learn."
How robots are helping solve China's elderly care crisis
The difference between humans and machines

As AI develops, it seems that the boundaries between humans and machines are becoming increasingly blurred. That is precisely why we need to talk about it, Doris Dörrie says. In her view, things become problematic "when we can no longer distance ourselves from technology and stop forming our own thoughts."

Human beings need to ask who we are and what truly defines us, Dörrie said. "I believe there is a major difference between robots and us, and that is the ability to play. A robot might be able to initiate a game, she explains, "but play itself is something profoundly human because it has no particular meaning or purpose."

Alongside these philosophical questions about what it means to be human, Dörrie makes a clear call for AI regulation. "At some point, we had to discuss nuclear weapons internationally, too. We've talked about all kinds of issues in the past, and we haven't just talked about them — we've also managed to find solutions," she points out.
"And I believe we need to move very quickly on this, too," Dörrie said.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: DOJ: Philippines has yet to criminalize foreign interference
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Thursday said the Philippines has yet to enact a law specifically defining and criminalizing foreign interference, pointing to gaps in existing espionage laws.

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 9:01pm
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Thursday said the Philippines has yet to enact a law specifically defining and criminalizing foreign interference, pointing to gaps in existing espionage laws.

During a Senate Committee on National Defense and Security, Peace, Unification and Reconciliation hearing on several bills concerning espionage, Senator Erwin Tulfo asked security agencies how they define threats to national security.

“We have not yet in our existing laws actually defined and criminalized foreign interference. We already have an established crime which is espionage. It's just a matter of Mr. Chair, of modernizing our definition of espionage,” DOJ Senior State Counsel Fretti Ganchoon said.

“Espionage is an established crime already, but with respect to foreign interference, we have not yet criminalized it. And so, if ever, this is going to be the first time that the Philippines will criminalize foreign interference,” she added.

Ganchoon cited a 2025 incident in which Chinese nationals were charged with espionage after they were arrested with equipment suspected of being used for spying. She added that the matter had not reached the DOJ.

She said the incident highlighted potential gaps in existing laws, particularly in cases involving the possession of suspected espionage equipment without the actual acquisition of classified information.

“Because indeed there are gaps in our laws… Perhaps it would be difficult if there's no actual obtention or getting of classified information in such a case and it's just mere possession of this equipment, Mr. Chair,” Ganchoon said.

Meanwhile, former National Security Council assistant director general Jonathan Malaya also said existing espionage laws were inadequate to cover certain acts involving sensitive government information.

“So, if an act of espionage is not committed against military installations—for example, [if it involves] secrets of the Department of Foreign Affairs, the Office of the President, or other civilian government agencies—that would not be covered by Commonwealth Act No. 616 or Article 117 of the Revised Penal Code,” Malaya said.
Enacted in 1941, when the Philippines was under US rule, Commonwealth Act No. 616 penalizes espionage and certain disloyal acts affecting the Philippines and the United States. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Starlink: How Elon Musk's company influences geopolitics
articles.summary: Designed to bring internet access to remote regions, Elon Musk's Starlink has become vital in crisis regions and war zones. But Ukraine also shows the risks of depending on the service.

image.caption: Starlink satellites have become vital means of communication in war zonesImage: Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Lack of internet access is a major problem in many regions of the world today.

Starlink was initially developed by the American tech billionaire Elon Musk to solve this problem. It was designed as a way of quickly getting the internet into regions all over the world where this was either impossible to do by conventional methods, or so expensive that it wasn't worth attempting.

blocks.caption: Starlink and SpaceX founder, controversial billionaire Elon MuskImage: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Since then, Starlink's field of application has widened significantly. It's used as a means of communication in disaster zones, but also by armies or protest movements, for example in regions where the existing internet has been destroyed by enemy fire or shut down by authoritarian governments.
But there is a downside: Ukraine's military, for example, is heavily dependent on Musk's satellite system. This has become especially apparent as the service faces external disruption.
How does Starlink work?

Starlink, which is operated by Musk's SpaceX company, is a satellite-based system consisting of 10,000 small satellites located around the world. They transfer data packages via laser links and do not require a constant, direct visual link to a ground station.

Unlike other internet satellites, which orbit at around 36,000 kilometers (22,000 miles) above the Earth, Starlink satellites are only about 550 kilometers up. This means they can transmit internet signals much faster than the others.

All users need is a small receiver terminal with an electronically controlled antenna, which automatically steers toward the satellites as they pass overhead. The terminals receive signals from these satellites and transmit them to a nearby router, which supplies the broadband internet connection.

blocks.caption: Starlink receivers smuggled into Iran enabled the opposition to organize despite the internet shutdownImage: Middle East Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Where has Starlink already been deployed?

Ukraine: Since the start of the Russia's full-scale war in February 2022, Starlink has become a vital instrument of communication in the war zone. The Ukrainian armed forces use Starlink to coordinate units, operate drones and control unmanned ground systems. In the civilian sector, the system is used by hospitals, emergency services, energy suppliers and the railway network.
Ukraine offers a particularly vivid example of how heavily its military capabilities now depend on Starlink.

In mid-October, Ukrainian army units reported disruptions to data transmission, which are said to have severely affected the control of combat, interceptor- and reconnaissance drones. Elon Musk said that restrictions on the speed and use of Starlink are determined by the US military and ultimately the US president. At this stage, it remains unclear who ordered the restrictions.

Iran: In early January 2026, protests erupted all across the country against the regime in Tehran. The government's hardline response included a nationwide internet shutdown. Reportedly, thousands of Starlink terminals were smuggled into Iran and sold on the black market. This enabled the protest movement to go on coordinating demonstrations against the regime, using Starlink to circumvent state censorship of the internet.
How reliable is Starlink as a wartime communications line?

The country's authorities are cracking down on the satellite service and its users. Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, the secretary of the Supreme Council of Cyberspace, described Starlink as a hostile "tool of war" and said the regime had means at its disposal to disrupt satellite connections.

Starlink is officially banned in Iran. Anyone using the service faces a prison sentence of six months to two years. If users are also charged with endangering national security or espionage, the offence can even carry the death penalty.

Sudan: In the Sudanese civil war, Starlink is used primarily by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group fighting against the internationally-recognized government. Hundreds of devices were smuggled into the country via the United Arab Emirates, and there is now a thriving black market for Starlink terminals in Sudan. The RSF use them to communicate and coordinate with their militias, while the Sudanese Armed Forces are trying to block both the import and use of the terminals.

Venezuela: Here too, Starlink has been used in the past to sidestep information blackouts and secure access to the internet. For a long time, the service was only available unofficially, by buying kits from local dealers. Following the US intervention in early January 2026, during which then-head of state, Nicolas Maduro, was taken prisoner, Musk offered the people of Venezuela a month's free broadband internet service via Starlink.

Gaza: Starlink has been used for humanitarian purposes in the devastated Gaza Strip since July 2024. Aid organizations and a field hospital use it to facilitate telemedical assistance and logistical coordination. Access for civilians remains limited because of Israeli security concerns.
Why has Starlink been criticized?

Starlink is often the only way to access the internet in conflict zones. This gives Musk and his operating company SpaceX tremendous influence. Previously, for example, Musk refused to activate Starlink in Ukraine to enable an attack in Crimea. US President Donald Trump has also threatened to switch off the satellites in Ukraine, as a way of forcing Kyiv to make concessions in peace negotiations.

blocks.caption: Starlink has provided vital communications for Ukrainian soldiers since the start of the 2022 Russian invasionImage: Alexander Polegenko/picture alliance

blocks.text: There has also been criticism from an ecological perspective. The Starlink satellites have a lifespan of less than five years. Every day, on average, one or two of them burn up in the Earth's atmosphere. This releases aluminum oxide, which could affect the ozone layer, contributing to global warming. In addition, all those thousands of satellites reflect the sunlight, making the night sky brighter, and this may also have repercussions for the world's animals.
Any Starlink alternatives?

In an effort to break Starlink's monopoly, other companies, especially in Europe, are already working on alternatives. At present, the biggest private competitor to SpaceX is a company called Eutelsat. With a fleet of over 600 satellites, its OneWeb service is far smaller, focusing on business customers and maritime use.

But Eutelsat is also involved in the development of IRIS2 — an acronym for Infrastructure for Resilience, Interconnectivity and Security by Satellite, an ambitious EU project to establish a highly secure satellite network. The aim is to make Europe less dependent on Starlink, but IRIS2 won't be fully operational before 2032.

Elon Musk also has competition inside the US from another billionaire, Jeff Bezos, whose company Amazon is currently working on Amazon Leo, known until recently as Project Kuiper. This is establishing a network of more than 3,200 new low-Earth-orbit satellites. Amazon plans to roll out the service later this year in the US, Canada, France, Britain and Germany.

blocks.caption: Chinese competition for Starlink and SpaceX: The launch of a Chinese rocket carrying astronauts to a space station in April 2025Image: Andy Wong/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The sky is clearly getting crowded. China is also refining two satellite communications systems of its own. Guowang, a state project conceived primarily for national and military purposes, will consist of up to 13,000 satellites, while another project, Qianfan, with an estimated 12,000 satellites, is more commercially oriented and aims to provide services to newly industrialized and developing countries. The first mass starts for both of these projects are planned for this year.
Will Russia have its own Starlink?
This article has been translated from German.
Editor's note: This piece was originally published on February 14, 2026. It was updated on October 15, 2026, to reflect recent developments.

articles.title: DOLE says AI not a threat but strategic opportunity
articles.summary: The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) said on Thursday that it is optimistic about artificial intelligence (AI), noting that it is not a threat but an opportunity to be treated responsibly.

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 8:32pm
The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) said on Thursday that it is optimistic about artificial intelligence (AI), noting that it is not a threat but an opportunity to be treated responsibly.

“We in the Department of Labor and Employment view AI not as a threat to be feared but as a strategic opportunity to be harnessed responsibly,” said DOLE Monitoring and Evaluation Division chief Hannah Gale Perea during the HR&WorkTech Summit 2026 in Quezon City.
According to the World Economic Forum (WEF), literacy on AI and big data is the number one fastest-growing skill by 2030.

“AI enables our domestic industries to transition towards higher-value services, moving up the global value chain into areas such as AI system oversight, complex analytics, and high-tier technical support,” Perea said.
But in the same report by the WEF, analytical thinking is the top skill needed in the workplace in 2025.
For its part, DOLE said that management of AI exposure in the workplace dictates whether it will result in displacement or employment transformation.
“By augmenting human capability rather than simply replacing it, AI can increase overall productivity, elevate wage potential, and improve working conditions,” said Perea.

The Philippine digital economy reached a Gross Value Added (GVA) of P2.74 trillion in 2025, accounting for 9.8% of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP), according to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) in April.
In 2025, the digital economy employed 10.39 million people, accounting for 21.2% of the country’s total workforce. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after school roof collapses in Pakistan
articles.summary: Rescue officials fear more people are buried under the debris in the north-western city of Peshawar.
articles.byline: Bilal Ahmed and Azizullah Khan, Phelan Chatterjee

blocks.text: At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials.
More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition. Several children are feared to be trapped under the rubble.
Emergency services were alerted to the incident at the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, a rescue official said.
He told the BBC the roof of an upper-floor classroom had collapsed, causing ceilings below to cave in as well.
Warning: This article contains distressing details
"The children in the affected [classrooms] were trapped under the debris," the official, Bilal Faizi, said.
The school is located in a building that had been constructed on a temporary basis, according to emergency official Arif Khattak.

Earlier reports suggested the affected classrooms were in a two-storey part of the building, but Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed later confirmed that classrooms on three floors had been brought down. There were about 30 pupils in the top class, 40 in the middle and 45 on the ground floor, he said.
It appears that when the roof of the upper-floor classroom collapsed, the falling rubble crashed through classrooms below, bringing their ceilings down too.
Saeed said the entire structure, which had "substandard" roof slabs, was "overloaded" and beyond the limit of how much weight it could bear.

articles.title: Hypersonic missiles highlight arms race on Korean Peninsula
articles.summary: Both South and North Korea have tested weapons feared by military planners for their speed and ability to maneuver in flight.

image.caption: Hypersonic missiles are far harder for defenders to identify, track and destroy [FILE: January 6, 2022]Image: YONHAPNEWS AGENCY/picture alliance

blocks.text: North Korea announced that it had tested two types of submarine-launched cruise missiles off its east coast on Wednesday — a day after the state-run Korean Central News Agency reported that leader Kim Jong Un had visited a new defense industry museum, where he admired an intercontinental ballistic missile reportedly capable of hitting targets in the continental United States.
The visit came five days after South Korean President Lee Jae-myung observed the test launch of his country's first domestically developed hypersonic missile.

South Korea's breakthrough came after Pyongyang announced a test on October 3 of what it described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile that traveled 350 kilometers (220 miles) before striking its target.

"Comrade Kim Jong Un expressed the expectation and belief that all the nation's missile forces would remain faithful to their missions of defending the sovereignty and security of the republic in a responsible combat posture," the KCNA reported.
'Advanced conventional weapons'
Both North and South Korea are primarily racing to develop hypersonic technology because it offers a step-up in offensive capabilities at a time of worsening tensions in the Indo-Pacific region.

blocks.caption: Pyongyang said it had tested two types of submarine-launched cruise missiles off its east coast on October 14Image: KCNA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Hypersonic missiles are weapons that can travel at velocities of at least five times the speed of sound (Mach 5) or over 6,100 kilometers per hour.

Their speed makes it far harder for defenders to identify, track and destroy inbound missiles, which can carry conventional or nuclear warheads. Their additional advantage over previous generations of missiles is their ability to suddenly change course, dip or weave in flight, making interception significantly more difficult.

"There has been an arms race on the Korean Peninsula for many years and hypersonic weapons are just the latest manifestation of that," said Chris Green, Korea Peninsula analyst for Crisis Group International.
Hypersonic weapons have become a "priority for the South" as the North has ramped up its capabilities and forged military and economic ties with Russia, he said.
"And North Korea has nuclear weapons, but it would not be viable to use them as the threat has always been that doing so would mean that the US would turn the country to glass," he told DW.
"For the North, it is unsurprising that the geopolitics of the region have encouraged them to pursue advanced conventional weapons as they try to have dominance on the peninsula."
What lessons is North Korea learning from the Iran war?
Pyongyang 'should not be underestimated'

And while it is impossible to confirm with any certainty that the weapons the North says it has developed have the capabilities they claim, Green said it would be a mistake to underestimate Pyongyang.

"We do not know their capabilities and it is possible this is all propaganda, but there is a long list of times the North's capabilities have been underestimated only to be shown that they can, in fact, do what they say."
Chun In-bum, a retired general in the South Korean army and now a senior fellow with the National Institute for Deterrence Studies, shares that assessment of the threat.
"It's anybody's guess whether they're telling the truth on this, but any prudent military planner should always assume the worst," he said.
The North's mastery of the advanced technology required to operate hypersonic missiles appears to have been sudden, although it remains unclear how it acquired the capability.

"They probably obtained the technology through illegal means," Chun said. "They snoop around firms in the US, South Korea and Japan for this sort of information, but they also do it to their 'friends.'"
Wherever the data came from, the fact that North Korea's hypersonic missiles appear to have performed as required should be cause for deep concern.

"A greater offensive capability increases the overall danger posed by the North, and if they have weapons that are harder to shoot down, then it is possible there are greater temptations to use them," Chun said.
"I'm speculating, of course, but I'm sure that we are looking at ways to neutralize this particular threat, but as I understand it there is no good answer right now," Chun added.
South Korea proposes talks to officially end war with North
Canceling each other out?
Green, however, believes that both sides developing viable systems means that they may cancel each other out as a potent battlefield advantage.

"I do not think this changes the balance of power," he said. "The North still has its nuclear deterrent and this 'porcupine strategy' of being sharp and prickly in order to keep everyone else at arm's length. And it's not a game changer south of the Demilitarized Zone either," the expert added.

"It is clear, however, that if the North continues to develop its offensive systems and is able to deploy them in huge numbers, then there will have to be a conversation about greater missile defense not only in the South but also in Japan, and that will then raise some very difficult questions."
